subsubtopic: EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I would like to present the following petition which deals with the massive reductions in education by the government, a little less than $500 million during the last budget.
These Canadians point out that these reductions, these cuts, are a contradiction of not only what was said in the throne speech, but also of the government's agenda with respect to increased productivity. How can you have increased productivity by taking those kinds of actions?

subsubtopic: EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have circulated a proposal for national education standards across the country as part of a private members' initiative. The response has been phenomenal.
I have with me a petition signed by people from Alma, Gatineau, Hull, Quebec, Saskatchewan and from my own riding of Ottawa Centre. All of these petitioners would like to see the House of Commons press the government to set national education standards in consultation and co-operation with the provincial governments, the territories and professionals in the education
field, as well as with the unions, parents, youth, non-governmental agencies and normal citizens. I submit this petition in accordance with Standing Order 36.

subsubtopic: EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the government the hypocrisy of its statements with respect to illiteracy and obliterating it in the near future.
Along with the increase in the role it wishes to play in education, it continues to tax books, which imposes ignorance on our population. Taxing books is a terrible mortgage on our future. It is hard enough to read and not watch television. We must make every effort to make reading accessible and therefore the petitioners call on the government to withdraw the tax on reading, the tax on books.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to continue in the throne speech debate where I left off on Thursday. I

May 21, 1991
The Address
want to reiterate that I see the challenge that we face in this session of Parliament as being threefold.
First, we must recognize the real limits of the capacity of Canada and Canadians to deal with change.
Second, we must pursue policies that will work to expand these limits.
Third, we must pursue these policies in a more open and more democratic way.
What does this mean in practical terms? Let me talk about one of the most pressing and tragic issues facing Canada today, one that concerns me greatly. At least one in ten women in Canada is battered by her male partner. A million women in Canada are battered weekly. Elalf of all women murdered each year die at the hands of their partners.
The prevalence of such violence in Canada is nothing less than shocking. Some say this violence is increasing as the advances made by women in society triggers a backlash, while others claim that the abuse women suffer at the hands of men is simply part of the uneven distribution of power in society. The challenge for everyone involved in this issue is to find a way of preventing the violence from occurring in the first place by changing deep-seated attitudes. We in this House can change laws in a matter of months, but attitudes, values and behaviour can take far longer to change. Recently our government announced a four-year, $136 million family violence action plan. The plan supports projects and programs that will increase public awareness and preventive action. Funding will be provided to women's groups and to other community organizations to raise awareness of family violence and to mobilize community action. We want to change attitudes that cause this violence, call the abusers to account and help the innocent victims.
I was pleased to see announced in the throne speech the appointment of a panel to inquire further into this serious problem of violence against women in our society. Government alone cannot ensure behavioural change, but it can certainly provide support to the important community work that is carried on every day; the work of community organizations and professional associations, schools and universities, the business community, and labour unions.
In other words, we are recognizing that real progress will take time and that the federal government does not have a magic solution. We are taking concrete steps to change peoples' attitudes, and we are involving a wide range of actors in the action plan: all levels of government, the voluntary and educational sectors, business and labour.
Another issue of concern, especially in these difficult economic times, is immigration. Like every member of Parliament, I see first hand in my constituency the human costs of an over-burdened system, separated families, and weeks, months and years for refugee status to be determined. Like every member of Parliament, I talk to constituents who ask why we are accepting so many immigrants when unemployment is so high. This is not such an easy question to answer sometimes. The arguments about future growth, the aging population, the need for certain skills and entrepreneurial talents and our duty toward the oppressed and the less fortunate are not always convincing for someone afraid of losing their job or afraid of different languages or cultures.
It is fair to say the stresses and strains placed on society by immigration policies are real. The impact of the refugee determination system on the health and welfare costs faced by provinces and municipalities is certainly real. The rise in public incidents of racism is certainly real. Perhaps we should take these as warning signs that the capacity of society to accept change is being tested and that we must find ways to review our ability to successfully bring new Canadians into the main stream.
The Speech from the Throne spoke of the importance of lifelong learning and of working to develop a learning culture in Canada. These are an important part of our economy and make us prosperous and more competitive. They can do this by increasing our capacity to adapt to change, to make the imperatives of the world economy a force for growth and for development.
If all the actors in the play-the provinces, business, employees, educators and students-can work together we can reach the goals that were set out: cutting illiteracy in half; doubling the number of university graduates in maths and sciences; quadrupling the amount of training in the workplace. It is important to stress once again that we do not want to turn the world upside down to revolutionize our economy or our system of government. After all they are only tools, tools that

are supposed to work for us, instead of us working for them.
It is the end result that matters; the happiness, the prosperity, the security of Canadians. Too radical change threatens this security.
Likewise, the inevitable changes that we will see in the next few years must be made to further our collective happiness, increase- our collective prosperity and enhance our collective security. We must all work together to pursue policies that will expand our capacity to compete internationally, to reduce and eliminate violence against women, and to develop efficient and responsive government institutions. We must pursue these goals in an open, fair and democratic way.
This means listening to Canadians, appreciating their dreams and aspirations, and recognizing the warning signs when change goes too far, too fast. This means that we, as members of Parliament, must act as the eyes and the ears and the voices of our constituents. It also means that all Canadians have a responsibility to actively join in the search for solutions and to become personally more productive, more tolerant and more involved in our community and society.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am very pleased to speak in this debate today on the government throne speech opening the third session of the 34th Parliament.
The throne speech contains three themes: unity, prosperity and government responsiveness. I would like to speak to each of these themes as an aboriginal person and as a northerner.
As an aboriginal person and a northerner, I am disappointed with the throne speech. It is basically a rehash of previous government commitments and a review of long-standing and on-going government activities. We have heard the promises about national unity, job creation and economic prosperity before. We have heard the promises about government responsiveness before. We we have seen them unfilled.
Aboriginal people and the north were mentioned in the 1989 throne speech, and I said then that I was worried about the extent of the government's commitment to northern and aboriginal aspirations. The govem-
The Address
ment's action in cutting programs for aboriginal people and northerners since 1989 has borne out my concerns.
This session of Parliament will be a critical session in Canadian history. The north and the aboriginal people are looking for more than just honourable mention in this government's agenda. We want to see concrete specific steps taken to include us as participants and not as mere observers or onlookers in Canada's constitutional renewal.
This government has several constitutional activities ongoing. The Spicer commission is to report July 1 and so is the special joint committee on the process for amending the constitution.
Aboriginal people and northerners have participated, albeit with some hesitation and concerns, in both these endeavours. Our reluctance to participate comes from a deep suspicion about where all this effort is leading and whether northern and aboriginal concerns are really going to be listened to and acted upon this time.
Where in the government's constitutional plans do aboriginal people fit in? We do not know yet, but aboriginal people must play a part, a pro-active part.
The new minister of constitutional affairs recently went to to both the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, and I commend him for travelling north so soon after his appointment. The minister met with only a few people and he is vague about the specific role he sees for aboriginal people and northerners. We still do not know how institutions will be reformed to better reflect northern and aboriginal concerns. We do not know whether northern and aboriginal people will have a participatory seat at the constitutional table. We do not know if the government is committed to completing the outstanding constitutional agenda of 1983 which is so important to northerners and aboriginal people. We still do not know if the government is committed to recognizing aboriginal self-government in the constitution.
I am pleased that the minister agrees that the north and aboriginal people have to be involved in the next round of constitutional talks. I want to urge the minister and the government to ensure that northerners and aboriginal people are involved in their own right and not as adjuncts of the federal government.

May 21, 1991
The Address
I have said before and I say again, this federal government cannot claim to speak for northerners and aboriginal people in constitutional negotiations. The failure of the last constitutional round proved this. The new constitutional relationship that aboriginal people and northerners are seeking must involve them as participants in their own right.
The government's constitutional proposal when it is unveiled, must reflect this necessity. If it does not, I predict more failure. Process, as the government should know by now, can be as important as substance. The process has to be fully inclusive, not exclusive.
In contrast to the views of the leader of the New Democratic Party, I believe politicians have a role to play in constitutional renewal. I see it, however, as politicians working with the people and not in isolation from them. It was the isolation of certain politicians from the people that caused the Meech Lake Accord to fail. This kind of isolation and ivory tower Constitution making must not, and I believe will not, happen again in Canada.
On economic matters, the government has asked Canadians, and I quote from the throne speech: "to participate in fashioning a new agenda for prosperity."
But how are northerners to contribute? Where is the assurance that the north will share in this prosperity?
The north is not mentioned in the government's economic discussion. It speaks of reducing interest rates and creating new investment, but where is the economic plan for the north?
The government is not offering to assist in creating a better climate for investment in the north. Where are the initiatives to help northern businesses reduce the cost of doing business?
Unlike the throne speech of 1989, this throne speech makes no reference to regional development. There is no discussion of the economic and employment needs of the regions in Canada, or of the impact of the current recession.
As a northerner, I cannot help but notice the emphasis on southern Canada. I do not see anything in this throne speech which would assist the struggling and developing economies of northern Canada. I do not see any initiatives which would address the serious employment needs of northern and aboriginal youth.
What we have seen in the past few years is the government's deficit reduction efforts being carried out on the backs of northerners. The goods and services tax is a prime example. Northerners are paying more than their fair share of the GST because the government refused to recognize the unique higher costs in the north.
This past February, the Liberal task force on the economy and the recession visited both northern territories. Our task force heard time and time again about the need for a substantial and revised federal commitment to the north.
The north's unique needs must be recognized by the federal government. Our people, our economic problems and potential are different from mainstream Canada. Federal economic policies must reflect and accommodate our differences.
This means making bold policy and program innovations based on the knowledge and experience of northerners. It means rejecting the old ways of twisting and turning northern realities to try to fit them into a southern Canadian framework.
These contortions do not work. Training, education and employment policies must be developed by northerners for northerners, not by southerners for northerners. I urge this government to adopt this approach as it ventures deeper into the field of education.
With respect to education, the problem is not so much one of money, as attitude. The throne speech talks about reaching a national consensus on performance, goals, partnerships and priorities for learning. The government should speak to the Ontario government.
The government suggests a goal of cutting illiteracy rates in half, but what is the definition of literacy? Is it the inability to read and write, or is it the inability to read and write English and French?
The government wants to double the number of post-secondary graduates in mathematics, science and engineering. Why then has the government been cutting research and development, science and technology funds since it was elected?
May 21, 1991

The leader of my party pointed out in his speech last week that despite the promise the Prime Minister made in 1984 to double research and development funding, R and D spending has declined from 1.42 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product in 1984 to 1.28 per cent today, a decline of more than 10 per cent.
We agree that Canada must position itself to participate fully in the global economy. There are opportunities we can seize, but these opportunities are not all in southern Canada. There are northern and circumpolar opportunities in science and technology and research and development which should be pursued.
I urge the government to include the north in its global strategic planning. It should not continue to let the Canadian north fall behind.
Northerners are somewhat sceptical about the proposed North American free trade deal. The Canada-U.S. deal did nothing for us. The government could have sought amendments to the Marine Mammals Act, but it did not.
I want to raise a concern as well about the effects on northern preference of the government's intention to eliminate hiring policies that give preference to provincial residents over those from other provinces. I hope that the government recognizes the large and special problem we have in the north of fly-in, fly-out workers and the pressing need to develop our own local trained labour force.
With respect to the environment, we have seen some backtracking by this government. The recent federal budget stretched green plan funding over six years instead of the five years promised initially. The Arctic environmental strategy, so important to northern Canada and to the world, is a step forward but a very small one. The funding, while welcome, is a drop in the bucket. The plan, for example, proposes cleaning up only 13 contaminated sites out of the 800 identified across the north, and there is much more the plan does not deal with.
The government's commitment to consult with aboriginal people on the terms of reference and membership of the proposed royal commission on aboriginal affairs is a positive one. The terms of reference as announced by
The Address
the Prime Minister in British Columbia, however, were too narrow. Aboriginal issues are not just social, cultural and economic issues. Aboriginal issues are political issues involving the fundamental relationships between aboriginal and non-aboriginal peoples and governments. The royal commission's mandate must reflect this.
But why did the government need to get such a high-profile person, namely the Right Hon. Brian Dickson, a former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, to serve as a special representative of the Prime Minister? This would seem to be an admission by the government that it does not have the credibility to do the job itself.
In addition, it appears the government did not consult aboriginal people on the selection of this special representative. The president of the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada issued a press release about this matter which reads:
Chief Justice Dickson's track record speaks for itself, but the fact that the Prime Minister appointed him without consulting us speaks volumes about the new respect for aboriginal people he claims to have developed recently.
The Prime Minister made a promise to consult aboriginal people about the royal commission, so he should have consulted us about the person he is delegating that work to.
The Inuit Tapirisat of Canada has every confidence in Chief Justice Dickson but is reserving final judgment, as I do, until it sees whether its recommendations to him are reflected in his recommendations to the government and whether the government implements those recommendations.
I want to comment here about the government's land claims policy. The government speaks of a reformed policy, but Canadians should know that the government has not reformed the basis of its land claim's policy.
If the government is serious about improving relations with aboriginal people, it must amend its claims policy. No amount of rhetoric about accelerating claims settlements will lead to the agreements the government says it wants, as long as the basis of the policy remains unchanged. There are fundamental problems with the current policy, foremost among them the continued insistence of the government that aboriginal people must extinguish their rights in claims settlements. The government must remove this offensive requirement immediately if it really wants to see progress made.

May 21, 1991
The Address
I urge the government to work with aboriginal people to develop a mechanism which would achieve certainty and clarity in claims settlements without extinguishment.
Aboriginal justice is another area touched on in the throne speech. The government says it will consult aboriginal people on changes in the system of administering justice. Given the government's track record on consultations, how serious is the government? Can aboriginal people believe the government is willing to make meaningful reforms?
The problems between aboriginal people and the justice system have increasingly come to the attention of the general public. We have had the Marshall inquiry in Nova Scotia. It said that the justice system failed Donald Marshall at every turn. Two recent reports have documented similar failures in Alberta.
Manitoba's massive aboriginal justice inquiry will report this summer and it will likely make the same condemnations of the current system.
Saskatchewan is beginning its own review. A meeting will be held in the north, in September, of provincial and territorial justice ministers and aboriginal leaders.
I would like to comment on another issue in terms of aboriginal justice that happened recently in British Columbia and Iqaluit. Kitty Nowdluk, who was a victim in a rape assault case, declined to testify in Iqaluit last year. Because of that refusal she had to undergo a very embarrassing experience when she was arrested in British Columbia. She was taken to Iqaluit through Edmonton and Yellowknife, back to Edmonton, over to Ottawa, and finally back to Iqaluit. She spent time in jail at every stop because she did not want to go to Iqaluit to testify in the rape case in which she was the victim.
She was made a victim of the circumstances and was treated as a criminal. How fair is the justice system when it arrests the victim instead of putting the criminal in jail? I wanted to comment on that while we were talking about the aboriginal justice system.
I want to conclude by making reference to the royal commission on electoral reform. This commission may recommend a process for aboriginal electoral districts as a means of securing more equitable representation for aboriginal people in the Parliament of Canada.
I would like to elaborate further on that electoral reform. I am a member of a committee that will be making recommendations on aboriginal electoral reform. The aboriginal people are going to be recommending that there be some means of ensuring more aboriginal participation in this House. The way to do that, we believe, is to ensure that there be some way of creating constituencies that reflect a large number of aboriginal people across this country. It does not mean, and I must stress this, that we want guarantees to ensure that aboriginal people get elected. What it means is that we want to ensure the process is there by which aboriginal people can get represented down here. We presently do not have that same problem in the Northwest Territories because the aboriginal people are the majority there. I urge this House to react favourably to the Electoral Reform Commission when it comes up with its recommendations.
I urge this Parliament to give this idea the thoughtful consideration it deserves as one means of changing the way Ottawa works for all Canadians and all aboriginal people.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with intrigue to the hon. member's remarks dealing with the throne speech. I have had the very distinct pleasure of being able to visit Cambridge Bay, which is about 2,000 miles straight north of the city I live in. I was absolutely amazed at all things I found in Cambridge Bay. I am not sure how close Cambridge Bay is to the hon. member's home.
Just to give some idea of how impressed I was, when you arrive in the community you find absolutely no roads, no fences, no power lines. It is a self-contained community. One immediately becomes very much aware of how difficult life must be, particularly given the harsh climate and the fact that the ability to produce things from the soil is not available to the community.
I noticed that the hon. member made reference to the fact that the throne speech did not make specific reference to assisting opportunities to become involved or to make jobs or work easier for employers. I note that is perhaps a much easier statement to make than it is one to put bricks and mortar to. For example, I met an individual who was the taxi operator, the day operator, a mortician, he dug graves, he was a general contractor
May 21, 1991

and on an on. It is tough to eke out a living in the north. There is certainly no question about that.
The hon. member went on to say that he is somewhat concerned with the elimination of borders, to bring in people to assist employers to provide work on the most cost-effective basis. I understand his concern with local employment, but on the other hand if business is to do business and be competitive, then I think they need to have all opportunities open to them.
He made some mention with respect to the Right Hon. Brian Dickson and his role and the system he has been put in charge of with respect to making certain things happen. He expressed some concern that, perhaps, this process did not proceed in a way he found favour with.
Therefore, my question to him is: If he were the Prime Minister and were to begin this process, how would he like this process to begin? How would he like to see this process evolve? Also, if he has time, what conclusions would he like to see?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I probably will not have the pleasure of being the Prime Minister in my lifetime, so it is a rhetorical question.
I just want to make a couple of comments. I am sorry that I missed part of the question with regard to the Right Hon. Brian Dickson. In terms of freeing the interprovincial barriers, one must realize that in the north today a majority of the construction companies or other companies that operate in the north started out from down here and have somewhat continued, although we are making great strides to get northern owned companies operating in the north.
When a majority of the companies are from down here, the thing that happens is that it is easier, cheaper for them to bring in their own people. In this case, I am talking about construction companies which are in the process of building houses and other construction. When construction workers come north, they leave home. They want to get back home as soon as possible, so they are prepared to work 16 hour days, long days, seven days a week.
The construction companies prefer them because they can finish the job faster and, therefore, the companies can make more money in the process.
The Address
As a result, the local people do not get as much of a chance to work for those construction firms as they would like because they have their own lives to live, they have their homes, and they have their families in that community. They have other commitments, whether it is in regional or municipal politics, and so have to do other work. They have outside interests other than the present construction that is going on.
I just wanted to make that point to show that the money that is spent is taken back out again because the construction firm and the construction labourers are not from that community. The money is used to build a house or whatever and is taken right back out again. Therefore, the money does not create the economic opportunities that it should.
I must make a further comment about the Right Hon. Brian Dickson. I never disagreed with his appointment, I just question the fact that the appointment was made without consultation with the aboriginal people.

Mr. Speaker, one of the things that this government announced last week, on Friday I think, in all its generosity, was that it had decided to maintain what is called a postal rate subsidy for food in the north. After the government cut it from $19 million, it will now be maintained at $15 million.
When we told the government that it should maintain the subsidy, it was adamant about eliminating it in the next 15 years. Keeping it is one way of ensuring that Canadians have a fair chance of being able to buy their produce and other food stuffs in the north in order to operate cheaper and better.

May 21, 1991
The Address
I believe there has to be more tax incentives introduced by the government, either this government or the territorial government, to ensure that northern companies operating in the north are better able to compete with the government, which is the largest employer in the north. We have a saying in the north that the private sector trains and the government hires. The private sector trains people to do certain jobs and then the government comes along, either the territorial government or federal government, plucks away those very people. That makes it extremely hard for the private sector to keep its employees and ensure that they have better productivity in the north.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise in the House this morning to speak in this debate on the Speech from the Throne and to express my full support for the objectives set forth by the government in this historic document.
As was mentioned by the Governor General, His Excellency Ray Hnatyshyn, national unity, prosperity, the environment and education are among the genuine concerns of Canadian men and women.
When I took up my new duties a few weeks ago, I had to go back to school, as it were, and read a number of papers.
One of these described Transport Canada's mission as helping to maintain a safe national transportation system that respects the environment and is responsive to the needs of a competitive economy and to the goals this country has set itself.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the department for which I am responsible is the linchpin of our action in this country. If there is any area and that is also valued as a symbol of the unity of this country, transportation is certainly one of them.
If we were to cross Canada from Cape Spear, Newfoundland, to St. Elias, Yukon, that would be a total of 5,187 kilometres. If we crossed Canadian territory from Ellesmere Island to Middle Island in Lake Erie, that would be a total of 4,627 kilometres. About 14 million people live in the narrow strip, 1,000 kilometres long, between Quebec City and Windsor, which represents
only 2 per cent of our territory. About 48 per cent of our population lives in Canada's 10 largest urban centres.
Mr. Speaker, one can scarcely imagine how strong our sense of unity had to be to forge and maintain the ties that keep this country together. I believe that sense of unity is still very much alive in the hearts of every Canadian in this country.
Since the beginning of Confederation, it was transportation that linked Quebec to the Maritimes, British Columbia to the Prairies, and Ontario to the East and to the West.
Historically, transportation has been one of the factors that helped unite this country. The construction of the railways brought the West into Confederation, and when we think of Canadian history, we often tend to think of those who built the railways as nation-builders. In fact, the railways started to expand in Canada during the second half of the nineteenth century when it was perceived as an important tool for uniting and opening up the country. Companies and private citizens started to invest massively in railway construction. The network extended in many directions and finally culminated in the transcontinental line built by Canadian Pacific.
When the "Last Spike" was driven in 1885, the railways became a symbol of the determination of Canadians. Has that determination disappeared? I don't think so, although Canadians may be less aware of it. We must therefore renew that awareness of their values, their strengths and their determination to be united with in a prosperous country.

Transportation was not only fundamental to the creation of our nation, but also has been and continues to be a mainspring of our country's economic growth. We estimate that the transportation services sector currently employs 700,000 people and generates $41 billion annually in economic benefits.
Transportation is more than just another economic sector. Since the earliest days of Confederation, the industry has been the main agent of the physical and political cohesion of our country. A strong and competitive transportation system is as necessary today as it was in 1867 to promote the development of all of Canada's regions.
May 21, 1991

Distance makes a transportation policy essential to our national well-being and influences our transportation priorities. Further, because the greater part of our country is so sparsely populated, domestic transportation is particularly important to strengthen our national unity, encourage national and regional development and provide services to remote areas.
We all know that Canada's economic future depends on our ability to compete internationally.

We believe that the planning of a new national rail system for freight transport complements the study of the national rail network and will help us develop an integrated surface freight transportation strategy.
The railways' rate of return for freight transportation was rather low in the past and there is no prospect of improvement if the present trend continues.
But those are not the only problems: Canadian ports have expressed many concerns about the competitive advantages that American ports enjoy and the possible diversion of containers destined for Canada to ports and railways in the United States.
The continued viability of Canadian ports as an essential link in the surface transportation system cannot be assumed. The success of our main ports on the east and west coasts is closely tied to the ability of our railways and trucking companies to provide services and rates that are competitive with those offered by American ports, railroads and trucking companies.
The task force report on Canadian ports that will soon be made public should provide an interesting analysis of the above issues and other aspects of the overall problem. The many interrelationships of the surface transportation system suggest that we cannot successfully meet all the challenges of transportation unless we consider the system as a whole.
Transport Canada is working on the first step of this strategy, which involves predicting what our surface transport system could be like and how it will function in a few decades. This document should be released shortly for comment to the railways, trucking companies, port authorities and provincial governments, among others.
The Address
We believe that this strategy will encourage intermodal transportation and help all modes of transportation look forward to a prosperous future and increased competitiveness. Our ambitions should not be limited by the size of our domestic market. Canada is home to some of the largest paper companies in the world and they produce twice as much wood as the Canadian market needs.
Canada is also the headquarters of one of the world's largest textile companies which earns 68 per cent of its revenue abroad. Bombardier sells 90 per cent of its transportation products abroad. I could continue this list for a long time.
All these industries contribute directly to the welfare of all Canadians. The government can help stimulate some of these industries and keep our industries competitive, but cannot do it alone. All concerned must cooperate, both private enterprise and workers and their unions. All those who are in any way involved with the country's productivity must work in the same direction.

Today, Canadians are increasingly concerned about their ability to compete. These concerns range from broad economic issues such as inflation, interest rates and the exchange rate to problems with our productivity performance like the effectiveness of investments, the burden of government and the business climate.
Government's have a responsibility to create an environment that encourages the growth of competitive and successful enterprises. The 1991 budget announced actions to restore fiscal balance and move toward price stability. This will lead to a stable-wide economic environment, increase the confidence in the Canadian economy and will strengthen Canada's ability to compete in a tough, economic world.
Boosting productivity growth and prosperity is far more than a job just for government. The private sector must take full advantage of the opportunities created by the actions of governments. In order to maximize productivity growth, the quality of investments in infrastructure, machinery and equipment, training, education and research and technology must be scrutinized. As well, consideration must be given to private sector spending in the areas of training and research and to other areas, such as education, where by international standards Canada's level of spending compares well but its performance does not. Prosperity and competitiveness are

May 21, 1991
The Address
not only issues for business, labour and government. All Canadians can help to strengthen Canada's competitive ability by identifying and developing an awareness of the problem. Only then can they be a part of developing solutions.

I hope that all Canadians, business as well as labour, are thinking about innovative solutions that will streng-hen Canada's ability to grow and regain the prosperity that made it the envy of so many other countries for so long. We are prepared to help Canadians explore new ways and new opportunities for cooperation between the public and private sectors to create a more favorable environment with a view to improving our productivity performance.
Cooperation could take the form of a partnership, for instance. We believe that it would provide a sound basis for solving common problems and face the challenges in an efficient way. The government is reaching out and I would like to give an example of this.

We are currently involved in negotiations to transfer the management and operation of several airports to local airport authorities. We expect the transfers to be completed by the end of this year at Edmonton, Calgary, Vancouver and Montreal. Aviation services, including air traffic control, airport safety and security, will remain the responsibility of the federal government.
The whole point of this initiative is to allow airports to respond more directly and positively to local communities' needs and interests and to encourage the national airport network to operate in a more commercial and cost-efficient fashion. It offers communities the opportunity to share in their airports' business.
The airport transfer policy announced in 1987 has sparked interest across the country and local groups are working with Transport Canada on similar transfers in Moncton, Quebec City, Windsor, Thunder Bay, Winnipeg and Kamloops.
The federal government earlier this year transferred 38 Arctic airports in the Northwest Territories to the territorial government. Last year, 10 other airports were transferred to the Yukon territorial government. Our objective is to establish a self-sustaining airport network that promotes increased local involvement while meeting the operational objectives of the national air transportation system.
I would like to address another matter, where partnership and co-operation between all parts of society is essential, and I mean government at all levels, industry and individuals, which is the environment. The government has already put in place a series of environmental partnerships involving individuals as well as special groups, the private sector, as well as municipal and provincial governments. Those partnerships extend to the international level. In the transport field, we must tiy to reduce the activities that are harmful to the environment. We must try to balance the demands for long-term development with environment consideration, such as noise, pollution and congestion. These factors will remain at the centre of our work and activities.
But there will be a price to pay. For example, last November the public review panel on tanker safety and marine spills response capability filed its report. It recommends, among other measures, the improvement of our capability to clean oil spills, the financing of research in the field of cleaning equipment and the assurance that in 10 years all tankers in use in Canada will be equipped with double hulls.
In a more general manner, my department will contribute to the environmental objectives of the federal government by proceeding with changes to regulation of the transportation of dangerous goods; responding to and implementing in conjunction with Environment Canada and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans the recommendation of the public review panel on tanker safety and marine spills response capability; working with the international marine organization toward development of an international convention on oil spill response; implementing the green plan initiatives which impact upon Transport Canada, including the federal code of environmental stewardship; the sustainable management program for the Fraser River Basin, the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence pollution prevention program, et cetera; contributing to the development of regulations pursuant to the new Canadian Environmental Assessment Act; reviewing departmental practices
May 21, 1991

and procedures to integrate environmental considerations into the decision-making process at all levels, in other words the airport group's environmental strategy; augmenting departmental work on environment protection through research and development like waste management, spills and leaks, long-term climate change and fuel efficiency; and finally by reviewing the regulation of vehicle emissions to phase in more stringent standards.
We hope, Mr. Speaker, that these actions will all contribute to the national effort to protect the environment and to avoid repeating past mistakes.
However, there is no magic solution to this tremendous task as many seem to believe. The support and involvment of everyone, at all levels, will be required.
I would now like to talk briefly about education, which occupies a prominant place in the Speech from the Throne. My concern for education dates as far back as the days when I was Labour Minister and will certainly not fade, because education is the cornerstone of any modem society.
As Michelet, the XIX century French historian and author, wrote in his book titled "The People":"What comes first in politics? Education. Second? Education. And third? Education."
The statistics quoted in the Speech from the Throne are unbelievable, Mr. Speaker: 3 out of 10 young Canadians do not graduate from high school and 4 out of 10 adults are virtually illiterate.
Canadian industry spends half as much on its employees' training as its American counterpart, a fifth as much as the Japanese and an eight as much as the Germans. That is terrible, Mr. Speaker, is it not?
How can we ask illiterate people to make a choice when in fact they cannot understand what is being asked of them? How can we ask young people to feel useful and proud when they cannot find a job because of lack of training?
The Address
I am from Quebec, Mr. Speaker, and I have never appreciated the federal meddling in education. It is clear that, to protect its language and culture, Quebec has to exercise an exclusive jurisdiction on education.
The federal government recognizes this and reaffirms its intent to respect provincial jurisdictions in that area.
It would be tragic, however, for the government of Canada to shirk its responsability to ponder over that whole question. Although statistics do not relate to one province in particular, they vary little from province to province.
In the context of a global economy, education and training needs know no boundaries. It seems perfectly logical to me to undertake a nation-wide discussion on the subject. Each province will then be able to choose among the proposed solutions the ones that fit their objectives.
Everyone's cooperation is urgently required, otherwise Canada will take a back seat to an increasing number of countries and will be incapable of taking up the challenges inherent to the pursuit of prosperity and quality of life all Canadians want.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I have to say a few words about Montreal, one of the most beautiful cities in Canada, and one of the most cosmopolitan as well. The ongoing development of the metropolitan area of Montreal is a main concern of mine and of this government.
What I has just said about education and training in the whole country also applies to Montreal, where the industrial structure is changing. Montreal youths have to be prepared to fill the high technology positions in the high-tech industries we have helped set up through our direct assistance. I am referring to research funding in the fields of pharmaceutical products, aeronautics and space tehcnology. It is imperative to prepare our youths to acquire expertise in these high-tech sectors.
In Montreal, multiculturalism is lived in great harmony. The social climate has always been one of tolerance and cooperation between its various elements. This is in line with the desire of Montreal to be recognized as a city of international status and to accomodate as many international organization's headquarters as possible. It has the full support of our government in achieving its goals.

May 21, 1991
The Address
Canada has always been a trading nation and a flourishing trade inevitably causes the movement of goods across Canada and a abroad. These operations cannot be carried out successfully without an efficient and competitive transportation system. A first-rate Canadian transportation system is one of the main components of a unified Canada. I undertake, as Minister of Transport, to do my best to promote this level of excellence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. There is much in the speech that one could speak on for quite a long time, not that the speech really has much substance. It does, however, touch base with a variety of issues that are important and deserve attention from this House and from members.
However, this morning I would like to touch on just two areas with which the Speech from the Throne deals. One concerns the question of national unity and the other area I would like to discuss is the question of productivity and economic growth.
First, concerning the question of national unity and the constitution and ways and means of getting constitutional change in Canada, I personally believe that what we need is a constituent assembly. I felt this way when Mr. Trudeau, of the former Liberal government, brought in its constitutional proposals. I believe a better way of dealing with a broad, sweeping change of our Constitution would be through some form of constituent assembly.
For a while, the then leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Yellowhead, supported that proposition. He advocated it for a short period of time, then he withdrew the idea. I thought he was wrong in withdrawing it. I wish he had continued to press for some form of constituent assembly.
What has occurred in the 1980s in terms of attempts at constitutional change just reinforces for me the necessity of having some form of constituent assembly. I believe our present institutions, Parliament and the provincial legislatures, as well as provincial and federal political parties are not suited to deal with the constitutional issue. I suggest that political considerations play a major part in our discussions and in our decisions concerning the Constitution. That is not surprising; whether we are

May 21, 1991
The Address
provincial or federal politicians, our concern is getting re-elected. That is the nature of the job and the role that we have. It is a job requirement, so to speak.
Our concern with the politics of it is an ingredient that is always there. I do not think I am divulging any caucus secrets, but when we sit around the table and discuss things like the Quebec veto, and I am sure this occurs in the Liberal and Conservative caucuses, a great debate occurs among the members, depending on the region you are from. The debate very often goes in terms of: "Can we sell this back home"? In other words, what are the political dimensions of this?
On top of that, going through the decade of the 1980s and toward the end of the 1980s, politics, political institutions, legislatures and parliaments have lost a lot of respect and credibility among Canadians. They see us very often as playing the political role rather than doing what the public feels is good for the country. In many ways this is simplistic, to be sure.
The fact that it is a widely held belief and feeling that we are just functioning for our own political interests and not for what is good for the country disables us from getting the credibility in dealing with this most important issue of national unity and the question of whether Canada, as we know it today, will continue to exist in the years and decades ahead.
My preference would be a process of consultation. All political parties on the federal and provincial levels would consult with various groups and get people from those groups to sit on a constituent assembly. We would have representatives from labour, business, the farming community, fishermen, women's organizations, native organizations, the arts, the universities and from a broad spectrum of Canadian society. The way I envisage it is somewhat similar to what many of the bands in my district have. There is the position called "elders", the elders of the band.
I would like to see a constituent assembly of elders from Canada to sit down-give them a year or two years-to discuss among themselves how this country can function. I would like them to get to know each other and the nuances of the various geographic districts as well as of the various specific interests and concerns that women, native people and that labour must have. Through discussing these interests and concerns, a
proposal can come forward in which there is equality and justice for Canada. They can propose a way of governing ourselves that would make sense and that would be acceptable to the Canadian people.
I would then suggest that proposals be put forward in a national referendum so that people supporting, advocating and educating the public on them would not be just politicians. They would be the representatives of the women's organizations, native organizations, labour, business and the various groups and components that make up our broad mosaic and are members of the constituents assembly. In this way, they would find the common concerns for example of women in Quebec and outside Quebec. The question of Quebec and the distinctiveness of Quebec would be reflected in their discussions.
Personally, I see this as the only means by which we could resolve the constitutional impasse that has been created for us. I must say this constitutional impasse has, to a certain extent, been the result of political considerations that were involved and which have created, to a large extent, the situation we are in today. I do not believe that our political institutions are capable of untying the knot that we are in now.
The other area I wish to touch upon is the question of productivity and economic strategy that the Speech from the Throne talks about. Again the Speech from the Throne talks in glowing terms. Often the rhetoric in the speech is correct.
I noted, as well, one part of the speech the Speech from the Throne calls upon:
Canadian business, workers and governments will be asked to work together to generate at least two and a half million new jobs by the year 2000 and to raise the real incomes of Canadians by at least twenty-five percent, by the same year.
In other words, the Speech from the Throne and this government calls upon business and labour to work together and to co-operate. That is a lofty notion. Excuse my cynicism when I hear it coming from this government.
This government has done more to alienate labour and to set one group of people in society against the other group in our society than any other previous government that I am aware of. This government talks about increased productivity and the importance of education. Excuse my cynicism, but this government has done more
May 21, 1991

to cut back on research and development, and postsecondary education than any government that I am aware of.
To be sure, I have not been here all that long. I have been here only since 1979, but I must say that in the 11 or 12 years that I have been a member, I have never seen such systematic cutbacks to post-secondary education, the science councils and the research councils than what has occurred under various budgets introduced by the government opposite.
There is no doubt that if we are going to survive economically, we have, as a society and as a country, to begin to focus our capacities and our assets as a nation. We must be able to bring private capital, labour, science, the public sector together to focus on certain economic strategies and goals. When you look at the successful economic models in the world today, whether they are Taiwan, Japan, Germany or other European countries, you would see, Mr. Speaker, that they have been so successful because they have been able to focus, to bring together and to harmonize the various assets they have as a country; to bring capital, the resources of the scientific community, and the public sector together to act as a co-ordinator and initiator and to ensure that public policy is in harmony with the goals.
To achieve that in this country I suggest requires quite a different attitude by this government. While this government might pay lip service to the goals, its actual record and its actual deeds have been the opposite. Rather than creating harmony, it has created disharmony; rather than being able to bring together and to focus, it has done the very opposite. It has split this country and its people into various factions and groups at war with each other.
As well, Mr. Speaker, when you look at the models of Taiwan, Japan, Germany and other European countries, you begin to notice that the public sector there plays a very important part. Even in Taiwan its steel companies are publicly owned because it fitted in with its industrial strategy.
This government opposite is so ideologically driven that it will privatize for the sake of privatization. It will not step back and ask the question: "Does it make sense
The Address
to have this particular enterprise in the public sector or not". It refuses to look at the question in this light.
The government is ideologically driven. It is part of the new right that assumes that any public involvement is bad. It says, just leave it entirely to the private sector and the private sector somehow or other will create new wealth and that new wealth will be distributed creating new jobs and opportunities and so everyone will be happy and well off. It is obvious that this has not worked.
If this government is serious about an industrial strategy, it has to drop its ideologically motivated and driven agenda. It is not appropriate in the 21st century. We have seen, mainly in the English speaking world, Canada, the United States, Great Britain, go through a new right era, the era of Ronald Reagan, the era of Maggie Thatcher and the era of this particular brand of the Conservative Party, which I hasten to add is different from the old Conservative Party of Stanfield and Diefen-baker.
This Conservative Party is the new right that originates in the United States. It has captured this party and has derailed it from the great tradition of the Progressive Conservative Party.
The type of Rambo capitalism this government encourages is not the model that would allow us to remain competitive, to have the leading edge technologically, to produce an economy that has decent wages, that has the production of new wealth in order for all of its citizens to benefit.
The first thing this government has to do, if it is serious about an industrial strategy, is to understand that the state does have a role to play in the creation of wealth as well as the question of the distribution of wealth.
We can also look at past Liberal economic strategies. Often, to tell the truth, they did not work that well. Quite often it was a case of throwing money at the problem. It was not all that smart. A lot of the money was wasted. It did not produce what the Liberals hoped it would produce.
The whole mad scheme that the Liberals introduced in the dying days of their government of the scientific research tax credit comes to mind. Billions of dollars were wasted, a terrible waste. It just benefited smart

May 21, 1991
The Address
accountants and fly-by-night operators who took advantage of this tax loophole. Had the billions of dollars been actually used in directed grants to our universities, to our research councils, we could have gotten much more benefit out of that loss of tax revenue.
The hallmark of Liberal economic strategy very often was waste. Money was given to people who did not need the money. Grants were given to certain businesses, and not to other businesses, which gave some businesses unfair competitive advantage over other businesses.
This practice continues with this present government. We hear stories now and then about certain businesses getting grants from the government, putting at a tremendous disadvantage that business' competitors.
The question arises whether the state should be involved in selecting winners. I would shy away from that. No, the state does not pick the winners. However, surely the state, in co-ordination with labour, business, and the scientific community, can select certain areas in which we can specialize, in which we can marshal our resources to ensure that we are successful in that area. The decision of picking winners is not one that a few bureaucrats in the government should make but a decision that should be made by a larger group of people in society.
The other thing that is important when we talk about an economic strategy or a social contract is that this government has to sit down and have some honest words with their business friends, and particularly Mr. d'Aqui-no and the Business Council on National Issues. It happens too often that governments, whether this government or the previous Liberal government, have given tremendous tax advantages or direct grants and loans to certain businesses, which then in turn have taken those gifts and very often moved south of the border. There is a certain social responsibility that requires that companies receiving special grants and subsidies or tax treatment remain in the country.
The other thing the government has to talk to its business friends about is their responsibility to pay their fair share in taxes. I am tired of hearing the business council and members of this country's large wealthy families lecture us about getting the deficit under control, while they who have benefited most from the
deficit, from the economic growth that has occurred because of the deficit, are the ones who pay the least in terms of taxes.
Talking about the types of rip-offs that occur, the Minister of Finance said in February of this year in a small press release, No. 91-018, Draft Legislation on the Income Taxation of Trusts, that when this legislation is passed by this House the government will defer billions of dollars of tax revenue that large wealthy families-the Eatons, the Bronfmans, et cetera-should start paying.
The Liberals in 1972 in their tax reform, when we changed from an inheritance tax to a capital gains tax, allowed the very wealthy families to defer paying taxes 21 years on their accumulation of wealth-the increase in the stocks and the bonds and the real estate that they held.
They were allowed to place that wealth into a trust, but there was a rule imposed that required them to start paying taxes on that wealth 21 years down the line. This government is now going to defer that for a whole other generation. I find that outrageous and obscene. If we are going to have an economic strategy with labour, management, business, and the public sector co-operating then everybody should also be paying their fair share in taxes.

First I want to take a moment and talk about Durham constituency, which I have the honour of representing here.
All of Durham constituency lies within the regional municipality of Durham. There are also within the Durham region two other smaller but more densely populated constituencies represented here by the members of the ridings of Ontario and Oshawa. Also one municipality in Durham lies within the federal riding of Victoria-Haliburton.
Durham is situated immediately to the east of metropolitan Toronto, and we have rich, rolling farmland and pine forests. Resort communities, such as Lake Scugog, are renowned throughout North America for their sports fishing. Also, Durham boasts a major industrial complex centred on the auto industry at Oshawa.
Durham is a community in which anyone would choose to live, so it is no surprise that it is one of the fastest growing centres on this continent. While providing ample space in which industry, commerce and families can prosper, it is readily accessible as well. Through it runs Highway 401 and principal transcontinental rail lines. GO trains and buses link Durham with Toronto and the rest of Ontario's heartland. Oshawa airport offers excellent passenger and freight service to more distant points. In short, Durham is open for business.
Anyone who gets to know Durham will agree with me that there is no better place to live, to work or to play. I say that advisedly. I have lived there most of my life and my family has been farming in that area for almost 200 years.
During the recent recess, we all had a valuable opportunity to get back to our roots, back to our constituencies, and to talk with the people we represent. That is an essential part of the democratic system. I want now to speak for a few minutes about some of the issues that are foremost in the minds of constituents, that concern me as a member of Parliament, and which I trust we will be addressing during this third session of the 34th Parliament.
May 21, 1991

As a member of Parliament, I am very pleased to see comments in the throne speech about increased independence of individual members in the House of Commons.
I doubt that there is a mature Canadian who is not deeply worried right now about our nation and how its future will evolve. It is all too easy to blame these worries on the present government and on the Prime Minister. I know many people do, including some members opposite. They are ignoring history and reality.
Finding ways to accommodate the demands of Quebec and French-speaking Canadians has been a top agenda item for every federal government at least since the quiet revolution in the early 1960s. Various approaches have been tried, offering Quebec particular status, seeking to make its people as one with other Canadians through bilingualism and guaranteed language rights. Succeeding governments had the best of intentions and wanted to make this work. Today, 30 years down the road, support for Quebec sovereignty has never been stronger and that province's future relationship with Canada is the most urgent question facing us now.
It is a complex question, as was detailed in last Monday's throne speech. All of us who have served through this Parliament are, or should be, aware that there are no simplistic solutions. I believe if we have a will to keep this country united, we can do so.
That is what I hope this session will achieve. I am sure that the great majority of Canadians feel the same way. We are seeking in the end a country which we each can love and cherish in our own way, though our reasons may differ due to our origins, our backgrounds, or the geographic regions in which we live. .Within that we want an equality that is qualified only in a very limited way for any group or region.
We have an excellent justice system built on heritage and tradition which incorporates safeguards to ensure fair treatment for all. It bothers me and many others to see these safeguards misused perversely. Our extradition laws should be tightened so they can no longer provide a haven at the expense of our taxpayers for those who enter Canada solely to evade criminal prosecution in other countries.
The Address
Surely changes are in order to prevent similar misuse of our generous immigration provisions for refugees. Almost every day we hear of cases involving those who enter Canada illegally and seek to stall extradition or deportation by claiming refugee status to which they are not honestly entitled, with the knowledge that the required hearings process will take months, if not years, during which they remain here, often at public expense.
One sometimes wonders whether the bar associations and law societies can condone the actions of lawyers who counsel clients to abuse our laws and the charitable instincts of Canadians in this way.
Preserving and improving our environment is a very broad concern. I am confident there is an ever-increasing public demand for action and results, which is how it should be. Our world is our most precious possession. Diminishing it in any way could only lead to our own destruction.
Our basic, continuing aim must be to leave this planet in better shape than we found it for the generations which follow us.
For Durham constituency, as for all of central Canada, improving the water quality of the Great Lakes must be a priority consideration. While much has been accomplished, we still have a long way to go. Although the levels of concentration of many chemicals in the Great Lakes have decreased significantly over the last two decades, they remain above acceptable limits.
Ottawa and other governments have recognized this. Canada and the U.S. have signed agreements aimed at eventually stopping the discharge of all pollution into the Great Lakes. This is a principal focus of the federal green plan.
In late 1989, the federal government announced a five-year, $125 million clean-up, with special attention to the most severely polluted locations in the Great Lakes basin. A recent agreement with Ontario will reduce threats to the waterways from high risk contaminated sites. Because virtually all the waterway is shared with the United States, what many of us want to see is a Great Lakes clean water agreement, similar to the clean air agreement for controlling acid rain and other airborne pollutants which was signed in March by the Prime Minister and President Bush. This agreement was only achieved as a result of some unusual high-powered lobbying of Americans and their elected representatives by our government and by dedicated public interest

May 21, 1991
The Address
groups. Similar action may well be needed to achieve international co-operation necessary for a determined campaign to restore the Great Lakes.
Man-made pollution is not the only problem. The St. Lawrence seaway and the international shipping it attracts have brought some natural threats to the ecology. One of these was the sea lamprey. A more recent arrival is the zebra mussel, which has begun to plug intake pipes, affecting drinking water and threatening the very ecosystem of some Ontario lakes. Research indicates zebra mussels and other foreign pests may well have come here in the ballast water of foreign freighters which was pumped out while the ships were on the Great Lakes.
During this session I hope to introduce a Private Member's Bill amending the Canada Shipping Act to require that all ships dump ballast water while on the high seas, before entering the St. Lawrence seaway and other inland waters, with a very stiff fine for non-compliance. This should prove a significant step toward protecting and restoring the ecology of the Great Lakes, a water system which contains close to one-fifth of the world's fresh water supply and which we have too long taken for granted.
Anyone living in or near urban centres has to be concerned about municipal waste and the resulting demand for rural landfill sites in which it can be dumped. In Durham we have had to contend not only with our own waste, but with growing pressure to accept massive amounts from metro Toronto. This almost reached a crisis stage. Fortunately, public awareness of the need to reduce, re-use and recycle and of the advantages of composting has been having a noticeable impact.
I think it is worth remarking here that by next year Durham region will have achieved a 25 per cent reduction in the amount of waste going to landfill, and fully expects to make that 50 per cent by the end of the decade. It demonstrates how strong the public concern is about waste and the willingness to participate when people are given leadership.
It is important that we follow the intent of the packaging protocol which has been established. It is even more important that individuals who have already reached a 50 per cent reduction in the volume of waste
leaving their homes be given leadership so they can go farther in reaching their personal objectives of minimizing household waste. I would suggest that we are now at the stage where legislation could be proposed and enacted, with the co-operation of the business community, to set specific targets and deadlines for eliminating unnecessary packaging. It need not be an onerous process. People want this. Smart industries will know that less packaging is the way to attract new customers.
In any discussion of municipal waste, another bugbear is so-called junk mail, the mass of unrequested advertising and promotion flyers which is delivered to our homes each day. Presumably it must be an important source of revenue for Canada Post at a time when it has begun to run in the black after decades of staggering deficits. Obviously, some people appreciate receiving this mail and respond to it. If it did not pay, retailers would not use this form of advertising. There are also a great many who abhor junk mail and they tell me about it constantly.
In attempting to deal with this issue, I think we should start by closely examining legislation that is now before the European Parliament to restrict the sale of mailing lists to direct mail organizations.
The European Community proposes that people must agree in writing before their names and addresses can be used in this way. One can anticipate the howls of protest from certain sectors of the business community. But here again, I believe they could be shown it would be smart and even profitable to stop antagonizing so many Canadians in this way.
My final words will be on the touchiest of all subjects these days-taxes. I want it understood that no one is more anxious to reduce taxes than I am. In that respect, it was my pleasure last winter to initiate and head a committee of our Ontario caucus that went through the Public Accounts of Canada and recommended a number of areas where substantial cuts should be made to federal spending.
Some of those were included in this year's budget. I regret that some other suggestions were not adopted, including cuts in the allocations for this House and its members.

I hope the Canadian public will understand just how effective this government's controls on federal spending have been. Average increases have been below 4 per cent, well under the inflation rate. Legislation outlined in the budget will restrict spending increases for future years and restrain future governments.
One might only wish that some other levels of government, including the province of Ontario, would show similar self-discipline. It is long past the time when all governments and elected public bodies must realize that, no matter how spending responsibility is rigged, jigged or shuffled about, it is the same taxpayers who pay the final tally. That includes you and me, everyone else in this House, and all the people across Canada.
The other day I spoke to an irate citizen who had just received his property tax bill. It was from his municipality, which is not in Durham, I might add. I am not sure that he did not hold me partly responsible. Certainly, he sounded so. He pointed out that his property taxes would be going up about 12 per cent this year, on the heels of a 10 per cent rise last year, with a similar 12 per cent tax boost forecast for 1992.
Yet, his personal salary increases for the past three years have barely kept up with the rate of inflation. My friend noted that almost 60 per cent of his mounting property tax is due to education.
The throne speech spoke of the "learning culture". We are putting enough money into education and retraining, but we must redeploy some of that funding to maximize the potential of every Canadian.
There is a basic message in all this, a warning which we can only ignore at our own peril. People are demanding governments that cost less and that tax less. They want government that is lean. If they do not get it, the taxpayers are going to become mean.
The taxpayers of Canada do not have deep pockets. In many cases, their fingers have already touched the bottom. Spending trends in Ottawa have been reduced significantly over the past six years. But more needs to be done. Now, other levels of government must recognize that the party is over and the onus is on them directly to stop overspending.
The Address
I have covered a number of issues in my remarks, all of which are important to me and to my Durham constituents. I believe the Speech from the Throne has outlined the correct course of action for Canada and Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member for Durham did speak about a number of things, as he indicated, but it seems to me that a major part of his speech was on the question of junk mail. I hope he does not think that amid all the problems we have in Canada today including national unity and economic problems, which I will get to in a moment, that junk mail is really a major concern of his constituents. Because if it is, they are certainly different from my constituents. For example, we have one in eight children who are allegedly not getting enough to eat in Edmonton and something like 50,000 people unemployed in Edmonton. I would seriously question whether his constituents' major concern is junk mail. If I misunderstand the member I hope he will correct me.
He mentioned that the party is over. But I would remind him that his government, which virtually talks about nothing but financial restraint to anybody who will listen, and not many people will, has added about $214 billion to the national debt of Canada, about $30 billion a year including this year.
I happen to have some statistics from the recent Economist magazine. I will just mention a couple of these things. Canada's industrial production for the last three months has gone down 10 per cent. That is one of the highest rates among the OECD countries. Our GNP is down 1 per cent on a yearly basis. Retail sales are down about 15 per cent. Unemployment, of course, is at 10.5 per cent.
The government is going to be massacred on this record in the next election, and I assume that the member will have something to say about these figures.
Let us take consumer prices. They are up on a three-month basis by 12 per cent. The only country that is worse than Canada in this regard is Sweden at 18 per cent. On a one-year basis, of course, prices are up 6.3 per cent. Again, only Sweden, Australia and the U.K. seem to be worse.

May 21, 1991
The Address
The current prime lending rate is worth noting at 10.25 per cent in Canada according to the Economist magazine.
What on earth does he think the people of Canada are concerned about, to end it? Does he think it is junk mail?
I am told that the member for St. Boniface will speak next on a matter of education. I might again ask the member, as I asked the last member who spoke for his party, the Minister of Transport: is he prepared to criticize the Government of Ontario which has the primary responsibility for education? Why, for example, is the Government of Ontario not prepared to take part in a cross-country test on the educational system?

speechtext:
I am quite happy to respond to what were, I believe, the questioner's three main points.
I have not gone back through my speech to check, but I believe I had two paragraphs on junk mail in a 20-minute speech, so junk mail was hardly a leading component of my speech. Possibly if the member represented an area just outside metropolitan Toronto, where just a few months ago six potential land fill sites were selected for receiving garbage from metropolitan Toronto, he would understand the sensitivity in those areas. Of course each one of those blocks represents hundreds of acres of prime agricultural land. Municipal waste, a small component of which is junk mail, is a very high-profile issue in my riding. Needless to say, the member is not aware of the significance of this issue in our part of the country.
I certainly have no problem resting my case on that particular matter.
As far as spending trends are concerned, any Canadian can check the audited Public Accounts of Canada and see the spending trends of Canadian governments of all political stripes since 1970. One will see I believe, since 1972 through to 1986, no government in Canada ever collected enough money to pay for programs, let alone one cent on interest and principal.
Any Canadian who has a mortgage and does not pay the interest or the principal for a period of something in the order of 16 years would have some appreciation of what their personal financial state would be. That is the situation in Canada.
Since 1986 we have been raising more revenues than we are spending on programs in any individual year, but it is still not enough to pay off interest on an old debt. In 1984, which was the worst year, there was a shortfall of $16 billion on programs alone, let alone the more than $22 billion shortfall on interest.
We have had a major turnaround, from running a tremendous deficit on operations to a surplus, but a surplus that still is not a big enough to pay interest on the old debt. Essentially, the build-up in total debt which occurred under the current government is compound interest accumulated on previously established debt.
While I wish that more could have been accomplished to minimize the impact of that compound interest, the facts are there for anyone to examine.
As far as the learning culture is concerned, I appreciate the comments of the member. I think the concept of the learning culture is much broader than just the educational system, although that is certainly part of it. It applies to the attitudes and the desires of individual Canadians to improve themselves at whatever job they may be doing or hope to do in the future. It does involve the entire primary, secondary, university, and subsequent retraining programs of one type or another that, as groups or individuals, we might seek to make use of. It is important that all governments co-ordinate their activities so that the money that goes into the whole learning process for Canadians is used for maximum benefit.
