speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to address the Speech from the Throne and I want to do so from two perspectives: first, what the address does not in fact speak to and, second, what the Speech from the Throne does address.
What does the Speech from the Throne not address? I think colleagues from all sides would agree that when one reads it very carefully there is indeed nothing that attempts to respond to the plight of the almost 5 million poor in this country, most of whom are women and over 1 million of whom are children. Neither does it speak to the difficulties suffered by the 2 million Canadians who are on welfare. That is most unfortunate.
May 21, 1991

Neither does it address the whole question of the food banks. You and I know, Mr. Speaker, there is an estimated 1.8 million Canadians during the year who will in fact be fed at those food banks, in a country such as ours which is considered relatively rich. By the way, it is important to note that perhaps 40 per cent of those individuals are children and young adults.
Neither does it address the question of the unemployed, the slightly more than 1.5 million people who are out of work today in Canada.
I was talking to a young woman during the weekend who desperately wants to work, desperately wants to find a job. She is extremely articulate, presents herself particularly well, and is anxious to work. There is no employment which is sufficient to help her raise her two children. There are jobs. Some of them are part time with minimum wages and poor benefits. That is unfortunate.
A week ago last Saturday, at an open house in my constituency, I met a young man who is well educated and has special skills in the area of marketing. He is a new Canadian and a member of a visible minority. He has been unable during the last 10 years to find suitable employment.
There have been short-term jobs but they have paid very, very poorly. There has been absolutely nothing upon which they could build a future. The Speech from the Throne does not address the plight and the concerns of those individuals and many hundreds of thousands of others like them.
The speech does not address the whole question of bankruptcies either which, if one compares March of this year with one year ago, have gone up over 50 per cent. What about those four small businesses in my constituency, the federal constituency of St. Boniface, that have gone out of business? What will it do for them? What will it do for its workers, for the men and women who were employed, some of whom were working for many, many years and now are without work, but who have families, who want what you and I want for our families, who want to be able to hang on to their homes, who want to be able to feel as if they can grow and prosper in our nation. The speech did not address the question of those bankruptcies where many people are put out of work.
Some members will recall my raising in the House of Commons the plight of almost 2,000 Canadians who were victims of the bankruptcy of Route Canada. We have tried every way to get the government to try to
The Address
respond to their needs. What has happened? It has shielded itself behind the investigations that are going on, rather than reach out to those men and women and try to make things right. These are men and women who had worked for many, many years. Some of them had no severance pay, no holiday pay. Some of them are still owed wages and other types of benefits.
Surely those are issues that touch the very fibre of what it is to be a citizen in Canada, and they might have been addressed.
What is there for farmers? I was speaking to a farmer yesterday who indicated to me that with the growing stress of attempting to run a farm in uncertain markets, with uncertain policies emanating from the federal and provincial governments, it is becoming increasingly difficult to operate.
What about small businesses? I met a proprietor of a small business just a few days ago in my constituency who said to me: "I wonder why I am doing this. When I look at the number of hours that I work, and when I look at the profit at the end of the day, at the end of the year, when I look at the red tape that there is with respect to a host of government regulations, both federally and provincially, when I look at the additional work that is necessitated because of the goods and services tax, I wonder why I am doing this. I," he said, "and many others are seriously considering whether or not we should continue to operate our own firms".
He asked whether there would ever be any relief in taxation because, quite apart from paper work, that is another issue. He pointed out that taxation had been increased not only at the federal level, but at the provincial and municipal levels as well. He was aware of the 34 tax increases that have been imposed by this government, which has made his workload much heavier, which has made his profits much thinner and which has increased the risks of operating a business.
This Speech from the Throne did not address the whole issue of day care for parents who need assistance. I met a young woman who was married and had a child. She is no longer with her husband and has an infant. She has a job that pays around the $6 per hour mark. She has no place to put her child. Even if there was, if she could find one, with the wage that she earns she probably could not afford it. Yet I admired the courage of this young woman. She was very young. She had a great deal of spirit, a tremendous determination. She simply wanted

May 21, 1991
The Address
to work and raise her child so that he could grow up and be a productive citizen.
In the Speech from the Throne there is no reference to recession. We are in a massive recession. We know that the deficit is in excess of $30 billion. It has been about that for a number of years. The debt will soon be $400 billion. That debt, which was less than $168 billion in 1984, according to a signed statement by the former Minister of Finance, is now going to be close to $400 billion. What does it do to allay the fears of Canadians with respect to that deficit and that debt?
Those are some of the points that the Speech from the Throne might have addressed, to reach out to Canadians and make them feel as if there was hope, as if there will be a tomorrow, as if things will fall into place, and provide them with some assurance that this great and prosperous nation will provide them with the opportunities they want and require in order to live in dignity.
What this Speech from the Throne addressed- [Translation]
National Unity. Some statements are fairly interesting; unfortunately, I think they are rather vague. I understand that the Prime Minister no doubt wants to have some flexibility but on the other hand, it does not reassure Canadians very much about what is happening. They are nervous. Obviously, they are very, very nervous. There is not too much assurance that linguistic minorities will not be sacrificed, an assurance that I would have liked to see in the Speech from the Throne. You certainly know that there are all kinds of rumours going around Canada that some fairly well placed people believe that one of the things that might be done is simply to sacrifice linguistic minorities, supposedly to make the country more united.
I would have liked to have a firm statement on the protection of linguistic minorities. And I can assure you that if support for linguistic minorities is ever removed, there will be a storm of protest across Canada because
these minorities have been protected, continue to be protected and want this protection to continue.
As for the bill or the initiatives that could have been taken on national unity, many people have noted that time has been wasted. They would have liked us to proceed as soon as possible, because if we continue according to the government's timetable, it is not impossible that once we reach the end of the tunnel, we will not have much time to correct the mistakes made along the way. It would be unfortunate to find ourselves in a situation where we would not have time to solve this major issue.

Another point made in the Speech from the Throne was participating in prosperity, la prosperite pour tous. The speech contained, and I understand that all political parties have a tendency to do this, exaggerated claims with respect to the Canada-U.S. agreement on trade and the benefits that another trade agreement with Mexico would bring. In the speech there is a comment with respect to the removal of interprovincial barriers. I find that extremely positive. I find though, that the exaggerations on the control of spending are really, really misleading. There have been reductions and they are around 3.7 per cent. However, let us admit that this has been achieved by cutting transfer payments to health and education. Who has picked up the difference? It is the provinces and the municipalities.
My colleague mentioned just a moment ago that people were complaining about the provincial and municipal tax bills. Of course, because the federal government has withdrawn. It turned over the cost to the provinces and municipalities which turned it over to the people.
Perhaps, the most glaring issue are the comments with respect to education, I do not mean to be unkind but they could be termed hypocritical. They are more rhetoric and the rhetoric has been excellent. It was excellent before the Prime Minister became the Prime Minister, when he was Leader of the Opposition. It was excellent before and during the 1984 and 1988 elections. However, nothing has happened except for massive cuts. There is flagrant contradiction in the whole area.
May 21, 1991

The Address
He talked increased productivity. We know that better education, training and retraining, research and development contribute to increased productivity. What do we do? Slash, slash. I have mentioned it so often. Cuts in 1986, cuts in 1989-1990, freezes for 1990 to 1995. During that period of time $10 billion, not million, fewer dollars have been targeted for education. No wonder the provinces and municipalities are suffering.
What about the reductions in research and development. What about the cuts in science and technology and investments in literacy?
The goals are laudable. I have to admit that, but there is nowhere any indication as to how the federal government is going to help the provinces or others realize those particular goals. I think that is unfortunate.
There was a lot of talk on the part of government in the Speech from the Throne regarding productivity and efficiency. That is a bit of a contradiction, some people would say a flagrant contradiction, because we have a government which says the right things but does the wrong things.
I understand very, very well that we have a serious financial problem. Are there not other ways to deal with the problem besides dramatically cutting spending on health and education?
['Translation\
Could other possibilities have been considered? Were there other alternatives? I think there could have been some. It is unfortunate that they claim to be controlling spending when they pass the costs on to the provinces and municipalities. We must look at it in terms of revenue, because as you know, revenue was over $70 billion in, 1984, I think, and now it is over $130 billion.
So there has been an extraordinary increase in taxes from all sides.

The goals, yes, they are worthy of being pursued, but we need less talk. We need action. We need to ensure that something is done, because our eroding competitiveness is directly related to a number of factors and one of those factors is our investment in education. Government is fond of saying:

-that investment in education exceeds that of most OECD countries. Yes, but be careful. The comparison is valid for elementary and secondary education, but less so for post-secondary. So let us make the distinction.
I know that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the other ministers are aware of the distinction. Do not try to fool the Canadian people, please. We must tell them the truth.
If I have time, Mr. Speaker, I will make a final point on the efficiency of government. The government says in its Speech from the Throne that it has reduced the number of Crown corporations by 24. Yes, but does it talk about the price paid in terms of efficiency, service and number of layoffs?
The government talks about 90,000 employees who were eliminated or cut. It talks about men and women as though they were products that are cast aside once they are used. But we must ask another question: Honestly, how much money was saved by cutting these 90,000 jobs? How many contracts were awarded to replace these employees? That is not discussed.
It is somewhat like the topic of job creation; we must also look at the other side of the coin. How many jobs were taken away? It is one thing to say, "A job is a job" but I can assure you that working full time for a reasonable salary with benefits that help us support our family is much better than something part-time at a very low salary.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue, but I have the feeling that my time is almost up. I see that I still have a little time left, so I will go on.
I will give a short summary. The Speech from the Throne touches on a number of issues like national unity, the economy, the efficiency of government and of course, education. These are all important topics but we must not forget, dear friends, that we must look not only at what the Speech from the Throne says but also at the issues it does not raise.
I just mentioned the unemployed, people who are fed by food banks, the poor; I mentioned those who live on social assistance; I also mentioned the small businesses and larger firms that went bankrupt and the people who

May 21, 1991
The Address
will go bankrupt. Canadians would have liked something to be said on those issues, but there was nothing.
I also deplore the government's trying to make Canadians believe that control on spending is much sounder than it is. The government should also tell them that although it has controlled spending up to a point, at the same time it has transferred the burden to the provinces, municipalities and people like you and me. I believe that is very important. When we talk about job creation, let us look at the other side of the coin. Let us talk about the number of jobs that were eliminated, let us talk about the number of jobs that were created, but let us also talk about the quality of those jobs and what that means for our constituents.
Neither must we forget that eliminating the Public Service raises another very important, downright fundamental issue: How much money was saved? Or were enough contracts simply given out to exceed any so-called saving?

When we look at the theme national unity, we have to ask ourselves questions about the massive cutbacks to VIA Rail, the privatization of Air Canada, the massive attack on CBC, the 20 per cent reductions in employment, 27 per cent I think it is nationally, and about 20-some per cent in Manitoba, what have they done to national unity. When we talk about economy and government efficiency, let us be very honest. Let us put the facts in front of the Canadian people so that they can understand what it is that you are trying to do and what it is that we are trying to do.
With respect to education, I understand it is always very, very tempting to say the right things. This, in a sense, is a win win proposal for the government because it talks about education, which is important to all of us: elementary, secondary and post-secondary, but actions speak louder than words and the actions have simply not followed the words.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of comments on the hon. member for St. Boniface's response to the Speech from the Throne.
He made some very strong innuendoes, in fact, accusations that the federal government is practising its restraint on the backs of the provinces and the municipalities.
I think the figures really speak for themselves. Over the last six years, government restraint has controlled our expenditures at 3.7 per cent per year. The provincial governments' growth in their expenditures has averaged 6 per cent and 7 per cent and in some provinces, as high as 10 per cent. There was absolutely no impact on the transfer to the provinces up until this year's budget and last year's budget.
Last year, he implied we had a massive attack and although there was an increase, it was cut back by a half of 1 per cent over what it was planned. This is far, far less than a massive attack on provinces and municipalities.
I would ask the member for St. Boniface if he feels that the provinces should continue to spend way in excess of inflation, way in excess of what the federal government spends and should they not have any sense of restraint in their own programs?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for the question. I note that it is posed in good faith. Clearly, I believe that all of us should be showing restraint, whatever level of governments we represent and whatever programs we tend to advocate.
At the same time, the government talks about the 3.7 per cent control of expenditures. I am sorry, I guess I did not make my point well The provinces are in the neighbourhood of 6 to 7 per cent. He is quite right. One of the reasons that the provinces are in that range is because of the massive cutbacks.
With all due respect to my colleague, the first cutbacks started a long time ago. For example, the most significant one was in 1986; 2 per cent cut in the transfer formula for health and education. That was followed in 1989-90 by another 1 per cent which was not executed because there was a freeze that came along for two years, which has been extended to 1995.
When I talk about massive cutbacks, that is another point I want to make. Not only the provinces and the municipalities have had to shoulder that additional load because they could not downsize quickly enough to accommodate that lesser revenue.
May 21, 1991

I mean it is very difficult to downsize the universities, the colleges, the schools, the hospitals and what have you. Not only that, but the other side of the coin we have to look at it in a more global context.
There are two issues here when you look at it in the global context. It is the accumulated impact of those reductions over time. Because the base is lower if you freeze it or cut it, the percentage increase over time is less. There is the double whammy if you wish. There is the accumulated impact of the cuts over time and there is the percentage increase which has been applied to a smaller base.
The point that I am making is yes, I agree with you that we must continue to show restraint. The federal government, to a certain extent, has shown restraint but let us explain to Canadians why that figure is as low as it is. Let us be fair with provinces and municipalities, and not dump on them without recognizing that one of the reasons that their taxation rates are going up-there are others-is because there is less assistance from the federal government and from the provinces as they tend to fill in that vacuum.
That is an extremely important point. It is not being made in a partisan kind of way. If you look at what I said, you will recognize that this is true.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, under Standing Order 43(2), I would just like to advise you that the government speakers-one from Wild Rose and the other from Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia- will be splitting their time so they will be going into 10-minute speeches with five-minute questions and answers.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the throne speech, our government proposed specific targets for Canada concerning the direction of our educational system.
As a result, our government has outlined educational goals and strategies that will lead us into the 21st century. Canada already spends more money per capita on education than almost any other industrialized country in the world.
Our review of educational performance has led us to ask why Canada as a nation does not appear to be getting a greater economic return on its substantial investments. Our government believes that educational goals reflect a
The Address
changing labour market. This does not necessarily require more funding, but rather a shift in emphasis toward a more active orientation.
As more countries become self-sufficient with agriculture and flood the world market, Canadian farmers will no longer be able to rely solely on agriculture in the future.
Technological advances and increased competitiveness reflect a changing labour market which demands a highly skilled and educated labour force.
Canada has failed to rank above the middle level in several international comparisons of student achievement in mathematics and science. We have a low rate of engineers and scientists in our work force. In particular, women account for only 13 per cent of the engineering degrees and 30 per cent of math and physical science degrees.
Canadian industry spends less than half as much on training its employees as American industry does, a fifth as much as the Japanese and an eighth as much as the Germans. This is not the kind of performance that will guarantee increased prosperity for our children. It has given rise to concerns whether the next generation of Canadian men and women will be the first to have a lower standard of living than its parents had. The challenge of Canada's training system is to provide individuals with ongoing opportunity to acquire productive skills that are needed in the marketplace. The focus of our government is to link educational and economic goals-specifically the future competitiveness of Canada's work force is in a knowledge-based economy. If Canada is to reverse its economic decline we must improve math, science and technology standards.
Canadian men and women must have access to both the skills and the life-long learning opportunities necessary to improve their job prospects and to ensure their own prosperity. Despite the great dedication of so many talented educators and administrators, Canadians are questioning whether the country's approach to learning is adequate for the future.
Our government recognizes that Canadians are concerned about education and would like to see Canadawide goals established for the year 2000. This will require provincial endorsement and co-operation.

May 21, 1991
The Address
Our goals include cutting illiteracy rates in half, ensuring that 90 per cent of Canadians attain high school diplomas or the equivalent by the age of 25, doubling the number of post-secondary graduates in mathematics, science and engineering, and quadrupling the training provided by employers to their employees.
Students and parents, employers and employees, educators and governments, will be asked to work together to develop a learning culture. Just as we have developed an environmental culture, we all must play respective roles in the future.
Continued prosperity depends on technological competitiveness and Canada faces a critical shortage of scientists, engineers, technicians and technologists in the coming decades. The role our government is playing to enhance our future competitiveness is to encourage studies in the natural science and engineering through the Canada Scholarship Program. This program will benefit 10,000 recipients, half of whom will be women.
We have also jointly developed a very encouraging program in several provinces to persuade young people to stay in school and complete their education. We have created Centres of Excellence programs which link Canada's best minds in universities and the private sector.
When unemployment insurance was first introduced, it was meant to be a temporary means of living while unemployed and searching for another job. There are now some Canadians who make collecting unemployment insurance benefits a lifestyle and it is at the expense of other Canadians. Many unemployment recipients feel a sense of helplessness and low self esteem when they are unable to qualify for various employment opportunities as a result of their limited educational background, which deters them from obtaining a job.
In the past, an unemployment insurance recipient was unable to upgrade the skills required to become more employable without jeopardizing the benefits. Our government realized that this unemployment cycle needed to be broken. As a result, we launched a major new initiative, the labour force development strategy, to help the unemployed acquire the skills they need to change with a changing world.
An example of such a program is the literacy training program for unemployment insurance recipients. Unemployment insurance recipients usually jeopardize then-benefits if they are not ready and able to work. Under section 26 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, people can now take certain types of training without incurring this risk. The new policy incorporates literacy and numeracy training into this category. A literate Canada will benefit both workers and employers alike.
We have done much but more needs to be done. The quality of Canada's human resources, a determining factor of our competitiveness and the engine of our future prosperity, is a national issue. It is not a federal issue, it is not a provincial issue, it is not entirely a governmental issue. It is a national issue and it demands a national response.
Co-operation will be critical. Federal and provincial governments, industry, the universities and consumers all have their roles to play. If everyone can work together on these challenges to reach a common goal, all Canadians in every region will benefit, now and in the future.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext:
I was quite impressed with the presentation of the hon. member and I notice she focused exclusively on education. She is to be commended for that. I would like to ask her whether she is aware that the private sector in Canada, particularly the companies that are involved in research and development in high tech, does not invest in Canada as much as other companies around the world do. That is because there is no national strategy that deals with the question of education or the question of research and development. There is no leadership on the part of the government whether we are talking about provincial or federal levels of government.
Rather than focusing all the time on the negative, I would like to mention on the positive side that we do have Northern Telecom, a leading company, not only in Canada and in North America but all around the world, which invests up to 9 per cent, even 10 per cent in some cases, in the area of research and development. That is a perfect example of the great success that our industries
May 21, 1991

could have internationally, only if our government provides them with the tools necessary with the proper method.
I would suggest that rather than waiting until the year 2000 in order to deal with the problem, we have to start now in dealing with the issues of illiteracy and education. By the year 2000, there will be over one million Canadians who will be uneducated and untrained and will not be able to enter the work force in a proper fashion.
Also by the year 2000, two-thirds of all jobs created in Canada will require more than a grade 12 education. So I would suggest that this matter is of great urgency and needs immediate action.
My question to the hon. member is: in her view, what is it the government should be doing now in order to deal with the problem we are faced with?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I want to thank my hon. friend and colleague for asking that question.
I feel very strongly that we have, up until now, recognized that there is a concern there.
We do need to have more graduates. We do need our young people to complete school, especially in the provinces that have not themselves dwelt that much on education.
The government, at this stage, recognizes that it is a problem. It is a problem today and it is a problem for the future.
I spoke of the year 2000. We are all looking now at the word "2000". We are looking at the future. We say 2000, but it is not something that will wait until the year 2000 to come into effect. We must start now. People in industry, the employers, are definitely losing the advantage by not putting more money into training their staffs. Yes, we are looking at training and will encourage employers in whatever is necessary. We will stress training over the next number of years leading up to the year 2000.
After visiting Taiwan I became very aware of the need for this country and for all governments, as my colleague has said, to work together. Both provincial governments and the federal government must work together because
The Address
Canada must enter the technological age and must concentrate on technology.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to participate in this throne speech debate concerning a throne speech which set out in general terms the direction for the next session of this 34th Parliament, the third session. This 34th Parliament may in many ways prove to be one of the most significant Parliaments, if not the most significant, in the history of our country.
The first session dealt exclusively with the ratification of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. The second session was highlighted by the passage, over the objections of an unelected and unaccountable Senate, of the goods and services tax legislation, the sales tax reform which had been due in this country for some 40 years.
This third session of this Parliament deals with the very future of the country itself. The three themes of the throne speech-unity, prosperity and government responsiveness-find themselves inextricably linked and intertwined.
There is an enormously high level of frustration experienced by Canadians today. A good deal of it is, I believe, economic. However, Canadians also want to feel that their elective representatives are hearing them, are listening to them and acting accordingly. It is clear, as well, that the deficiencies and the inadequacies of a Constitution framed in the 1860s, and modified somewhat 10 years ago without the support of a province which contains some 28 per cent of the population of the country, must be addressed. It is time to shake off the post-Meech doldrums and move to make the changes necessary to our Constitution.
The message from Meech Lake was twofold. First, Canadians wanted into the process. They felt left out. The decision-making seemed too remote. Indeed, after the midway point, December 1988, and the passage of Bill 178 in Quebec, the process was not in keeping with the wishes of the majority of Canadians. Those concerns which arose half way through the ratification process made it, I believe, politically impossible for any province which had not by that time ratified the accord to ever do so.
The second message is one of fairness and equity. Whatever one province is seen to achieve through the process must also be available to others. There must not

May 21, 1991
The Address
be any particular special status for one province or another, no deal for one that is not available to the rest.
That is why the federal government must and will ensure Canadians the opportunity to participate fully in this process of constitutional renewal. This is being done and will continue to be done through a number of commissions and fora.
The citizens' forum, while obscenely expensive, can nevertheless claim that it has received input from literally hundreds of thousands of Canadians. I believe that there will be some useful input coming forward from it when the report is filed on or before July 1.
Also due on July 1 is the report of the Beaudoin-Ed-wards joint Commons-Senate committee, which has been charged with the responsibility of finding a way out of the impasse, to find a means to achieve constitutional change.
At present, constitutional change requires in many instances the unanimous agreement of the House of Commons, the Senate and the 10 provinces. This requirement for unanimity has caused a constitutional log jam.
It is rather difficult to go into the room to talk about constitutional change when the door is locked tight and no one can get in. To get the door open, we need a key and that is where the Beaudoin-Edwards committee comes in. It will find the key that will open the door to constitutional change.
Once these various reports are in and the government has a chance to digest them, the government will lay out proposals to focus public discussion on the goal of a more united Canada. In doing so, it is important to remember that what we have right now is not all bad. Relative to the rest of the world, Canada is in pretty good shape.
I come from an area on the prairies in Saskatchewan of some 25,000 square miles which is overly dependent on the growing and marketing of grain. My constituents tell me overwhelmingly that they want a continuing strong central government: one capable of setting and maintaining national standards; one capable of managing the eighth largest economy in the world; and one that is capable of responding to the needs of a particular sector or region when it finds itself disadvantaged, as all the regions and sectors of our country have found themselves from time to time.
In Saskatchewan, in my area particularly, we have a very cyclical economy. Sometimes we are on top of the world and are putting in through equalization, and other times-now being one of those times-we take out. That message comes to me clearly from constituents.
They want to get rid of duplication and waste, they want efficient government and they do want to see some decentralization out of Ottawa to the provinces and to the regions of the country.
The objective is not to throw everything out and start over again, but rather to modify and seek change in order to build on and improve that which we already have: a nation which, from the outside looking in, is the envy of the rest of the world. Residents of many other nations would give their eye teeth to enter this country.
The proposals generated over the summer months, after the reports of these various commissions, will be referred to a joint parliamentary committee which will be established to consult with Canadians. This referral is to take place by the end of September.
The committee will then have five months to travel within Canada from sea to sea to sea. It will meet in public session with provincial and territorial counterpart committees.
After receipt of the report in February of next year, the government will propose a plan for a renewed Canada for the consideration of all Canadians. There will be legislation to provide for greater participation by Canadians in the process, if indeed this is necessary.
I believe also that the time necessary must be taken. The unity question must be dealt with in a measured way which permits ample time for input from Canadians every step of the way. Only in this way will the end product be capable of acceptance by the great majority of Canadians.
National unity and economic prosperity go hand in hand and there can be no doubt that insofar as the future is concerned, investment decisions both in Canada and abroad are affected by uncertainty. Interest rates are affected because investors want certainty, stability and sound management.
