subsubtopic: REVENUE CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government has a policy of hiring at Revenue Canada's Data Taxation Centre in Sudbury which discriminates against non-residents of the city and district.
In the past year we have lost over 2,400 of the 4,000 mining jobs at Elliot Lake and we will lose over another
1,000	jobs next spring. This community is hurting, with homes, careers and even lives being lost in the turmoil created by the mine closures.
When one of my constituents applied for a job at the Data Taxation Centre in Sudbury, he was told that he must live in the Sudbury district to be considered for the job. This person is a Canadian citizen. He pays taxes to this very Data Taxation Centre. He needs a job.
I call on the government to stop this irrational, unreasonable and unfair discrimination against unemployed Canadians seeking a job. The government's hiring policy is simply wrong.

Mr. Speaker, I recently met with members of the Jewish students group Nahon. These students are among many who are very concerned about the oppression of some 4,500 Syrian Jews.
There is an urgent call for action against the Syrian government. Jews are forbidden to leave Syria, they are being tortured and jailed, they are not allowed to vote and their homes fall victim to random, unwarranted searches.
The Jews of Syria are being denied basic rights that are set out in the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights which Syria has signed. The Government of
Canada has always supported the cause of oppressed Jewry and human rights.
Today, along with members of this House, I call on the government of Syria to comply with the UN declaration and allow those Syrian Jews, who wish to emigrate, the right to do so freely.

Mr. Speaker, during the weekend Canadians were informed that this government is once again secretly considering closures of Canadian forces bases in five communities across the country.
Communities in the Atlantic provinces, already suffering as a result of the recession, stand to be the hardest hit. Three bases are being targeted in that region alone.
Canadians know the economic ruin that befalls a community when its major employer is suddenly removed. In these difficult times, the last thing Canadians need is for job losses and upheaval as the government makes piecemeal decisions about defence spending.
There is no doubt that defence expenditures must be reduced. These kind of secretive, ad hoc decisions, however, serve neither the local communities nor our national defence policy. We call on the government to undertake an immediate, thorough review of Canadian' defence policy before any closures are considered and to assure Canadians that viable alternative economic opportunities will be provided to communities in the event base closures are necessary.

Mr. Speaker, families have changed drastically over the last century or so. Today they are much smaller and they tend to scatter across the country rather than stay in a single location.
Taxation has changed as well. Unfortunately, the changes in taxation have not reflected the changes in the family. We now have a situation which penalizes married couples and gives a tax advantage to singles living together.

May 21, 1991
I am sure that each one of us in this Chamber is deeply disturbed by the erosion of the family as we have known it. Do not let us contribute to that erosion through lack of legislation.
I am very much encouraged by the throne speech, in which the government promised to review our policies in relation to the family. I am very proud to be part of this initiative. I believe strongly in protecting the interests of the family, for it is the very foundation of this great country.

Mr. Speaker, in the past year, rumours of base closures in Atlantic Canada and rumours about military cuts in general have created a climate of anxiety in my region.
Canadian Armed Forces personnel are understandably anxious and worried about where they might fit in the crunch that appears to be on its way.
Armed forces personnel are not alone. The closure of bases in the Atlantic region will be devastating for an economy already hard pressed by government policies to date.
If the reports prove to be true, the provinces of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, in particular, will be hurt by loss of personnel and a loss of spending dollars and a loss of spin-off jobs.
Air force bases, particularly in Nova Scotia, are an important part of Atlantic Canada's lifeblood. They are also part of our history, our industry and our well-being.
We ask that this government take a long look and think hard before adding more fuel to the fire that is burning up the economy of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the work accomplished by native people in remote localities, by native businesses, airlines, merchants, provincial and territorial officials who, through extensive consultations with the government of Canada and the
task force, made it possible to stabilize the postal subsidy for the North at $15 million.
Without this subsidy, the price of perishables in most localities of Northern Quebec would far exceed the prices being paid in areas such as Central Arctic. For example, one litre of milk could cost $10 and a loaf of bread $7.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the hon. Tom Siddon, and his team, but caution will be required in standardizing postal rates.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recent reports in Kingston suggest that budget cuts at federal penitentiaries may negatively affect public safety.
Corrections Canada employees are, like all public servants, suffering at the hands of this government. To date, 59 positions have been eliminated in the Kingston area alone. By reducing staff there will be fewer guards on duty. Each guard will have to man more shifts. This will lead to overwork and increased stress. In a prison environment, this will in turn create greater tension between guards and inmates and lead to dangerous confrontations.
The federal government's attempts to reduce the deficit by attacking public servants is deplorable. However, by cutting prison staff, the government is not only attacking its employees it is also creating a potentially dangerous situation.
I therefore urge the government to listen to the Union of Solicitor General Employees and provide each institution with the funding it needs to adequately guard federal inmates. The safety of the public and the safety of the staff may be jeopardized if the government does not act.

Mr. Speaker, whatever one may think of the Belanger-Campeau report, it clearly identifies Quebec's concerns with our 1982 Constitution Act.
May 21, 1991

First, the report makes clear that the principle of equality of all Canadians enshrined in the Charter of Rights does not make allowance for special constitutional recognition for Quebec society.
Next, the principle of multiculturalism enshrined in the charter implies that the French language and culture are on the same footing as other languages and culture and does not require special guarantees in our Constitution.
Finally, the principle of equality of all 10 provinces enshrined in the amending formula of the Constitution implies that any power granted to Quebec must be granted to all other provinces as well, thereby conflicting with both the concept of a unique Quebec and with the views of the proponents of a strong national government.
Essentially, Belanger-Campeau identifies the fundamental differences that haunt our country, differences that we must resolve if we are going to continue to have a strong and united Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the matter of national unity. I would like to express the concerns of thousands of Canadians who are outraged by this government's dismantling of our national postal service.
To date, over 950 federally owned and operated post offices have been closed or privatized. Many of these closures cause hardships for residents who deserve first-rate postal service and are losing postal service altogether. Many of these people are our seniors and handicapped people.
For many communities, the post office is the only visible federal presence. After gutting the CBC and VIA Rail, this government will deal another serious blow to Canadian unity by closing down hundreds of post offices.
On behalf of the residents of communities like Avon-more, Ontario; La Redemption, Quebec; Mabou, Nova Scotia; Brandon, Manitoba; and Pitt Meadows, British Columbia, I strongly urge this government to stop post office closures and to work to improve our national postal systems.

Mr. Speaker, the latest VIA Rail annual report proves that the government did the right thing when it forced it to slim down before it would suffer a heart attack. Here is some good news. First, customer complaints went down 60 percent last year, while praise for VIA Rail and the new service it offers increased substantially. Second, the on-time performance of VIA trains increased from 65 percent in 1989 to 80 percent in 1990.

In fact, the only bad news in the VIA Rail annual report was about passenger revenues during the first half of 1990 which were below the targets. The only reason for that was the negative publicity created by the Liberals and the NDP surrounding the introduction of the new service.
Shame on the opposition on that question.

Mr. Speaker, Saturday evening in the Montreal Congress Centre the national Quebec tourism award ceremony was held.
I am very proud, Mr. Speaker, to report to this House today that Abitibi-Temiscamingue won top honours at that occasion, as the International Film Festival of Abitibi-Temiscamingue was awarded the most prestigious award, that is the Prix de ['excellence touristique (award of excellence in tourism), for contributing over the past ten years to the Quebec cultural and tourism recognition. This high distinction crowns ten years of efforts and relentless work to turn a regional festival into a national and even international event.
So, I want to congratulate, in my name and on behalf of my constituents, all the organizers of this festival for this great success. Well done!

May 21, 1991

Mr. Speaker, after studying and hearing countless witnesses last spring on Public Service 2000, the public accounts committee had very serious concerns about the so-called reform to the Public Service.
It strongly recommended that before proceeding with legislation or administrative changes, the government should establish a special committee of this House of Commons and should refer all recommendations from Public Service 2000 to that special committee.
The white paper on Public Service 2000 was tabled over five months ago and yet the President of the Treasury Board has still failed to heed the advice of the public accounts committee of this Parliament.
By stomping all over collective bargaining rights, gloating over thousands of lay-offs, spending countless taxpayers' dollars fighting court cases on equity and fairness in government, the government has proven beyond a doubt it knows better how to dismantle, destroy, and demolish than how to build a nation.

Mr. Speaker, without question the very fibre of our society and family life is being threatened by an ever-increasing criminal element goaded on by suggestive pornographic material so readily available in video shops and on our bookshelves. Despite the efforts of many concerned people, hard core pornography still exploits children and degrades women. It is a frightening reality that child abuse and battery of women is on the increase.
We heard in the Speech from the Throne the importance of protecting our children and the stability of family life. I have heard from many constituents who believe that tough legislation to control the distribution of pornographic material is a necessary step in ensuring our children, our women, and our society have the protection they deserve. We have not yet put this
legislation in place. Let us not continue to delay. A strong and healthy Canada depends on it.

Mr. Speaker, like my father before me, there are tens of thousands of individuals waiting to adopt Canada as their home. There are tens of thousands of families waiting to be reunited with their loved ones. There are tens of thousands of refugees waiting for their first hearing.
Canadians and immigration applicants certainly would like to know, in fact they demand to know, how it is that Mohammed Al-Mashat managed to jump the queue and get through the entire immigration process in just 28 days, leaving them behind.
The tens of thousands of immigration and refugee applicants want to know-actually they are now fully aware of-the motto that this government has on immigration policy: It is not who you are or how desperate your case, but who you know.

Mr. Speaker, as a reward for their responsible and competent gulf contribution our armed services are going to be rationalized and down-sized. This is sneaky and ominous bureaucratic fuzz for saying that cuts are coming that will adversely affect Canadians from coast to coast, including my native province of Nova Scotia, where we have had a history of servicing the services that has been a long and time-honoured military tradition, and whose economy very much depends on servicing the services.
So far, all we have had are rumours and resignations and silence from the minister. Surely before any decisions are made there has to be an open and thorough debate of defence policy. Canadians must be involved and what better way than through the new parliamentary committee on national defence. The committee's first priority next week should be public hearings on this vital issue and they could do no better than to start in my home province of Nova Scotia and perhaps in its shire city of Halifax.
May 21, 1991

Mr. Speaker, each spring the Porcupine caribou herd migrates past the most northerly community in my constituency, Old Crow, as they make their way to calving grounds on the Arctic north shore. For 20,000 years the Gwitch'in people of Yukon and Alaska have depended on the Porcupine caribou herd for their livelihood, all the while practising sustainable development in its purest form.
In 1980 the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge was established to protect this way of life from exploration and development. But this could all change. President Bush wants to open up the refuge for oil and gas development and a key committee of the U.S. Senate is to vote on this matter today.
I call on the ministers for external affairs and environment to meet with their U.S. counterparts to reinforce that exploration in that refuge is simply unacceptable to Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. On the weekend the Prime Minister said during an interview that Canadians were responsible for the present economic and constitutional situation. When will the government stop blaming Canadians for the present situation and act responsibly, since this government is responsible for the serious problems facing this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is true that we are going through some difficult times. We have a very serious slowdown in the economy and the unity of the nation is under question. Obviously it is going to require a broad-based public debate to deal with all of these issues.
Oral Questions
The issues we face are very complex. They can only be resolved on the basis of Canadians working together in a partnership. I think we have to draw all Canadians into the process, to come forward and be a part of the solution. We must deal with the issues in a manner that is traditional and in keeping with the Canadian way of life.
I sense that the Leader of the Opposition has indicated his full co-operation in addressing the issues that confront Canadians. I welcome that and look forward to his co-operation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say the Prime Minister is quite wrong to blame Canadians. Canadians are not suffering from a lack of affection for their country, they are suffering from a lack of affection for this government.
Today the Conference Board of Canada said that the recession will be much worse than had been predicted only three months ago. It said that seven of ten provinces would experience negative economic growth this year.
When will the minister realize that the economic policy of this government is a great failure? The government has given us a new Minister of Finance. What we need is a new set of economic policies. If the Minister of Finance wants our co-operation, he should listen to us, reduce our interest rates so they are more competitive with those in the United States, reduce the Canadian dollar to improve the competitiveness of Canadian goods and services. Then we will be on the road to recovery. But he should listen to us once in a while.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
I am sorry that the Leader of the Opposition gets political on this very important issue. However, it allows me to say that during the time when he was the Minister of Finance the Bank of Canada rate climbed from 7.5 per cent in September of 1977 to 11.25 per cent in May of 1979.
What has happened with this government is the fact that interest rates have gone down by 5 percentage points over the last year. There is clear evidence that business confidence is improving, housing starts are improving, housing sales are improving, automobiles sales are improving, the unemployment figures are going down, not up. There are some positive signals on the horizons, Mr. Speaker. I don't want to be over-optimistic

May 21, 1991
Oral Questions
but I want to assure my hon. friend that all the indicators are leading in the right direction.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we thought we had a new Minister of Finance, but this is the same old stuff that we heard from the previous Minister of Finance. I would like to tell him that when I was Minister of Finance Canadians were working.
Hear, hear.

At that time, we had Canadian economic policies.
I would like to know from the new Minister of Finance when he will take his responsibilities seriously. If this government decided that we need a new Minister of Finance, it is because we need new economic policies. When will the Minister of Finance do his job?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of the fall-out of the policies of the Leader of the Opposition when he was in the government and occupying the position of the Minister of Finance, we saw the unemployment rate at that time at 12 per cent. It was 16 per cent in the province of British Columbia. It is considerably less now. Canadians and Canadian enterprises have created 1.6 million jobs in a climate that was positive.
We have serious inflationary pressures which must be addressed. The hon. Leader of the Opposition knows that very well.
I regret very much that he does not like me being a bit old-fashioned, but I can tell him that unless you get the fundamentals right and unless you deal with the underlying causes of inflation, inflationary pressures and expectations, you will not be able to bring interest rates down. If you are not going to bring interest rates down, you will not have a turnaround in the economy.
I repeat again, we are heading in the right direction. All the indicators suggest that, and the hon. Leader of the Opposition is just going to have to be a little more patient because when we get the fundamentals right, the Canadian economy will start to grow again.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport and it relates to the crisis faced by the Canadian trucking industry.
As the minister knows, last week the human face of the difficulties and frustrations facing Canadian truckers was brought to Ottawa and is still here for all to see.
The minister subsequently met with the workers. We debated the issue in this House. We, the Official Opposition, offered the minister and the government a package of alternative options that can work if put to use.
Therefore, I ask the minister whether the government is finally prepared today to announce some immediate relief measures that will serve to alleviate the overwhelming burden that truckers face as a result of the policies of this administration.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to report that over Wednesday, Thursday and Friday of last week, I and the officials from my department met with the spouses and the truckers themselves to examine this situation.
The conclusions of these meetings according to my officials are to the effect that two sets of recommendations have been outlined by the owner-operators. The first set is what one can call the political agenda in that they are going back to the free trade agreement, the GST and deregulation of the industry.
As far as the GST is concerned, I said last week in this House that there is nothing wrong with the GST as far as the trucking industry is concerned. For one thing, the tax on fuel has been reduced by 2.5 cents per litre as a result of the implementation of the GST.
As far as deregulation is concerned, there is no intention on the part of this government to go back on the question of deregulation. From all quarters, we are hearing that deregulation has been veiy beneficial to the Canadian people as such.

Mr. Speaker, the minister must be talking to American truckers because they are the only people who have gained from deregulation, not Canadian truckers.
May 21, 1991

Oral Questions
Not only has this government been hiding behind seven studies for almost a year, but we have gone through one week of protest, discussion and debate and the minister continues to abdicate responsibility and fails to show key leadership at this critical period of time.
I return to the minister. What is it going to take to wake up this government and to resolve this issue immediately rather than hiding constantly behind studies? Temporary relief measures, even at that, are not incompatible with his studies.
Can the minister tell this House when the truckers can expect some real action, some real solutions and some real sensitivity to Canadians for a change?

Mr. Speaker, I mentioned before that the recommendations were of two orders during the meetings last week. The second order is related to the operational costs of the truckers. We have examined many of these issues and found at the end of the day that the recommendations today are exactly the same as those which were made by the representatives of all segments of the trucking industry last year. Those recommendations gave rise to the formation of a task force that is made up of all representatives of the trucking industry.
The owner-operators on the street at the present time refused to be part of that coalition. That coalition and all the other segments of the industry are saying today they are in agreement with the processes that have been implemented. They agreed to have these seven studies. These studies are going to be released on May 27 and the task force is going to meet on June 4 and 5 to make their recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. There is one thing that no study needs to be done to tell us, and it is that these truckers parked outside this House and many like them across this country are losing their homes. It is creating many family problems and truckers are losing their businesses. We do not need a study to tell us that.
There are two concrete things this government can do. One clear problem that the truckers have is related to the GST and the fact that they have to wait five to six months for any rebate. This costs them thousands of
dollars, which they have to put up front. I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister whether he will not ensure that those rebates can get to those truckers when they need them and second, whether he will acknowledge that the deregulation policies brought forward by the previous Liberal government and continued by his government will be reviewed and regulations brought in so that Canadians truckers can compete in the Canadian market?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I simply want to remind the leader of the New Democratic Party that the GST replaces the federal sales tax. The truckers paid federal sales tax before. They did not get any rebate. They had to swallow it. In the case of the GST, they get it refunded as an input tax credit so it really does improve their competitive position in that it does reduce the cost of doing business.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is clear from the personal instances that we have seen what this government's policies have done to the independent trucking industry.
The trucking industry is one industry that has been devastated by this government's policies. The steel industry is another, particularly the policy of the U.S.-Canada trade deal. This week the United States Congress decides whether it will give the fast track to the trade talks. I want to ask the Acting Prime Minister what work the government is doing now to ensure that in two years' time we will not have another devastated industry lined up on Wellington Street because of the policies that this government is pursuing around the trade deal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I again want to remind the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party that transportation was not a part of the free trade agreement, so it has nothing to do with the allegation that she suggests.

Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the transportation industry is not on a level playing field in Canada. My question to the Deputy Prime Minister was simply, what preparations is the government doing, given that the United States is going to fast track the Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade deal? But on another subject-

May 21, 1991
Oral Questions

Carla Hills, the U.S. representative at the tripartite negotiations, has confirmed that the United States wants to put culture on the table. Ms. Hills suggested that culture could be adequately protected with cultural exhibitions. Will the minister confirm that culture will never be part of two-way or three-way free trade?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party knows full well that the government's position on this has not changed. Culture is not on the table, never has been and never will be.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. In his absence, I will direct it to the Deputy Prime Minister.
This weekend there were press reports of a recommendation to cabinet that included closing Canadian forces bases, two in Europe and a number all across the country. In view of the fact that Canadian forces performed so admirably in the gulf, and in view of the fact that many people want to know their long-term security at those bases, will the minister confirm or deny these reports? Will he say why the government continues to operate on ad hockery and will he say why it refuses to bring forward a defence policy for this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that my hon. colleague recognizes the very important role that our Canadian men and women played in the gulf. It was interesting to note this weekend the accolades which our naval personnel received.
With respect to the defence policy review, yes, indeed, and I think my hon. colleague would agree that the changing international situation, the changing fiscal situation, requires us to look at the future of defence policy in this country. That work is under way. Based
upon changing assessments of threats and new roles for our people, decisions will flow from that about the appropriate size of the force, the appropriate infrastructure and equipment that will be required for the future.
Until cabinet has had an opportunity to look at those proposals, it would be inappropriate to discuss any specific aspects of it. Following those discussions, of course, I am sure my colleagues will look forward to discussions about the future defence policy for this country.

Mr. Speaker, the international situation may be changing, but it is changing in this country to getting worse. We are in the middle of a recession now and there are areas that depend economically on defence establishments.
Will the minister give an undertaking that before any changes are made in defence policy, there will be a full review which will be in consultation with all the people of Canada. Will she give that undertaking?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Obviously, in looking at a defence policy for the future, there are many aspects that must be considered: the international situation, Canadian security, the numbers of people and roles they must play.
I think it is evident, though, and I am sure my hon. colleague will agree, that some changes to infrastructure will be required. In fact, we are looking at all aspects of infrastructure. In looking at that, of course we look at the social and economic effects of changes in our infrastructure, and that will be part of the considerations that will come into our cabinet deliberations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Over and over again, this government has told Canadians that the GST is revenue neutral. On November 12, the Prime Minister said in Calgary that the GST would not cost Albertans a nickel more than they now pay. But today the truth comes out. The Consumers' Association of Canada reports today that 72 per cent of products
May 21, 1991

monitored by them have cost more than the government promised they would.
My question to the Deputy Prime Minister is this: how can he possibly reconcile the statements made by the Prime Minister, in his home province of Alberta, with the facts as they are presented to him today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it might interest the hon. member to know that the Consumers' Association of Canada just issued a news release which indicates that this is not an official study by the Consumers' Association of Canada.
What they do say is that the Consumers' Association of Canada believes that Canadian consumers deserve a full and comprehensive quantitative study on the impact of the GST on prices in the Canadian marketplace. We agree with that.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Deputy Prime Minister should get his quotes straight. It says:
This has not been released as an official study of the Consumers'
Association of Canada at the present time.
My question to the new Minister of Finance and Deputy Prime Minister is this. Will he please tell us which of the only two possible scenarios could explain the startling discrepancy in facts? Either the former Minister of Finance could not count straight or his government misled the Canadian public about the disastrous effects of the goods and services tax on their own pocketbooks.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are ways to get around making statements and putting questions which are unparliamentary and I do not want the hon. member skating too close to the edge.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member refuses to deal with the present. He may want to take the House into his confidence and tell us whether he would rather deal with the past or the future.
Oral Questions THE ENVIRONMENT

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of the Environment.
Canada's forests are being overcut according to the majority of professional foresters, and Japanese corporations are leading the pack with activities that would land them in jail at home.
Will the Minister of the Environment ask our Prime Minister to deliver a message while he is in Japan this week that clear-cut logging inside our largest national park, Wood Buffalo, is unacceptable and that Daishowa should stop that activity, that clear-cutting 40,000 square kilometres of Alberta without an environmental assessment is unacceptable and Daishowa should stop, and polluting the Peace River upstream of Wood Buffalo National Park and many Northwest Territories communities is unacceptable and Daishowa should stop those kinds of activities in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to say today that the member is being consistent with himself in statements that he made last week in the House of Commons. They seem to be blanket statements that do not always correspond to the facts.
I think the record will show that, as far as this government is concerned, we will have been the government to have created a full-fledged Department of Forestry to deal with issues directly related to forestry, to have brought in a green plan that brings together sustainable development, to make that happen for Canadian people, and that, in this context, we intend to deal with all forestry issues as they come along.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to hear that this minister has crawled under the same blanket and he endorses foreign nations logging inside our national parks.
I have a supplementary. Mitsubishi and Daishowa are clear-cutting 120,000 square kilometres of Alberta, an area one-third the size of Japan. They will pollute the Peace River and the Athabasca River upstream of our largest national park.

May 21, 1991
Oral Questions
Will the minister send a message along with our Prime Minister for the 10 days that he is in Japan that Albertans and Canadians care about the environment and when a project like Mitsubishi's ALPAC is turned down by a federal environmental assessment, no means no, and this new Minister of Environment will stand behind decisions that are made by panels, not beside them like his predecessor did?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think we need any lessons insofar as dealing with the environment is concerned. We need to take no lessons from the hon. member or people from his own party.
The member will also know that certain projects that he is referring to have gone through environmental assessments and they have been dealt with at both provincial and federal levels. There are assessments that are there, there are processes that are there now that are even under review, that there will be legislation and has been legislation brought before this House to deal with environmental assessments. All these projects and future projects will be dealt with with one single important consideration in mind that all members share around this House and that is with dealing with the environment and sustainable development.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment.
Last week, the Federal Court of Appeal ruled that the James Bay Agreement has force of law. As a result, the minister not only has the authority but the obligation to take his responsibilities seriously. This judgment is a clear contradiction of the agreement signed with the former minister on February 12 to split the Great Whale project study.
Mr. Speaker, my question is this: Could the minister confirm that the study will not be split, and that infrastructures will not be separated from dam construction? Could the minister confirm that he will reject his government's unsavory policy on the Great Whale project?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can inform the hon. member that I had a meeting last Thursday with my colleague, the Quebec Environment Minister, representatives of Inuit groups and representatives of the Cree.
To my knowledge, Mr. Speaker, it was the first time all four parties were around the same table, and it was at our request.
At this meeting, Mr. Speaker, we reached the following consensus, and this includes my Quebec counterpart: everyone agreed that for environmental purposes, it made more sense to conduct the study on the Great Whale project as a whole, instead of splitting the project in two for this purpose, as had been the case.
Mr. Speaker, it was not our decision to split the project study in two. After last Thursday's meeting, I can also inform you that my Quebec counterpart intends to have a meeting with the parties-with representatives of his own government-to find out whether there is a possibility to consider the project as a whole for environmental purposes.

Mr. Speaker, that is certainly not the report we had on that Thursday meeting. The Minister of the Environment of Quebec has stated unequivocally that the problem he is having with his own cabinet arises out of a lack of support from this government for the environment. That is very clear and this minister is not going to get away with that kind of insipid, weak-kneed response.
The minister either takes a stand now or he stands forever condemned, along with his predecessors.
The issue is very, very clear. The Federal Court of Appeal has spoken. It said that the 1975 James Bay Agreement has the force of law. It has the force of federal law. This government has the right to move.
The only question in this House is: Why will this minister not stand up in this House and state unequivocally that this government will stand behind its own laws?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know where the hon. member pretends to get his information.
I was in a meeting with my colleague, the Minister of the Environment for Quebec and with representatives of the Inuk and of the Cree, no later than last Thursday night.
As I have already said, all parties, including the provincial minister, agreed at that meeting that for environmental assessment, it was a lot better to undertake an assessment based on all of the project and its cumulative effects, rather than split the project in two. I
May 21, 1991

Oral Questions

Hear, hear.
was very happy to hear that coming out of the mouth of my hon. colleague of the environment for Quebec.
He also undertook at that meeting to go to his own government to try to see whether it could change its approach vis-a-vis this project, which we were very happy to hear. We will see what the outcome of that meeting is and we will then go on to deal with the environmental assessment of the project.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Recently a member of this government admitted that the average processing time for a Canadian citizen to be reunited with a spouse married abroad was 900 working days.
Many of these Canadians were devastated to learn that Mr. Al-Mashat and his spouse were admitted in just 28 days.
I ask the minister why his government has fostered an immigration system that offers special treatment for the elite but only delay and despair for ordinary Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member thinks that she is helping Canada by trying to portray our immigration system as a system favouring the elite over poor people, then I submit with respect that she is not helping her country, Canada. We have no such system in this country.
Last year, 212,000 people immigrated to Canada and they were not all former ambassadors.
The situation of Al-Mashat is going to be looked at by a standing committee of this House and it will do its task.
The answer to the member's question as to why will be answered then. Please, do not tell the world that in Canada we favour the elite over ordinary people who immigrate to Canada according to the rules.
The last refuge of a scoundrel is an appeal to patriotism.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would put her question.

My supplementary is for the same minister. At the commencement of the gulf war, the then Minister of Employment and Immigration delivered a directive banning the issuance of visas to Iraqis and Palestinians applying for entry into Canada. Clearly, in the case of Mr. Al-Mashat, who was admitted before a formal cease-fire was signed, this directive was ignored. Does the minister expect Canadians to believe that his officials in Vienna would override a specific ministerial directive during a war without the knowledge of his predecessor?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to note that there was some discussion in the House on this topic last week and there was an agreement forthcoming from this government that all the issues related to this matter would be discussed in committee. We are looking forward to being at that committee, both my colleague and myself, and all the relevant officials.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. When I called the minister's 1-800 line regarding the Meme implant, it was still using figures saying the risk of cancer to women with Meme implants is equivalent to smoking one and a half cigarettes in a woman's lifetime and refers to only one in a million women facing cancer from the Meme. The FDA in the U.S. is saying one in 10,000, but some scientists from the FDA are stating one in 50, or one in 100.
Will the minister tell Canadian women who to believe and what is the minister planning to initiate to clarify for Canadian women the wide-ranging disparities coming from scientists?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, first of all, in response to my first question as minister of health and welfare, I would like to say that my primaiy interest is the health of Canadians, particularly women in this case. I think all

May 21, 1991
Oral Questions
our work, as minister responsible for the department, is for the health of Canadians.
In this case I believe that everything has been done to be as up-front as we could in terms of the information provided. The 1-800 line has been used over 500 times since it has been put in place a couple of weeks ago.
In the medical world, decisions are made in light of information that is available, and I believe that in terms of breast implants that is the basis on which our decision has been made. In this case all information available is referred to the department and, when necessary, we duplicate the control to be sure that the information is the best and we will continue to do that.
In light of the information that we have, a decision will be made in light of the health of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the minister's answer. However, I think it important that we be aware that when there was nothing out of the FDA, this government was waiting for the FDA for stats. Now we have stats from the FDA that say one in 10,000, and some of the scientists are saying one in 50, one in 100, and we are still saying we are using the best information available.
In light of this, I would like to ask this minister if he will make an undertaking that the kinds of projects that Dr. Chan from Calgary, and other doctors who want to do research into the safety of implants, will be funded as soon as possible. Will he give women of Canada that undertaking?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the department received in March the study by Dr. Chan from Calgary and we are dealing with that project. Dr. Chan himself said that he believed that more study should be done.
The hon. member is are asking me for an undertaking on funding. I have not personally received any request from Dr. Chan to provide any help. If this should be the case, we would consider it. There are many researchers in this country who are independently doing this type of research and refer to the department all instructive information that could be provided. We will continue to do that.
First of all, what Canadians, particularly women, want in terms of that issue is the best information available. It is what we do and the department is open to anyone who wants to check if what we are doing is well done. There is no problem with that.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister for International Trade, whomever he or she may be today.
A long time family-owned sawmill business in the upper Ottawa Valley which under normal conditions employed about 300 people has closed down its operations, taking 12 million badly needed dollars out of several small communities.
When is the government going to wake up? When is it going to get rid of the 15 per cent export tax? When is it going to lower the high Canadian dollar and give the forest industry and the forest workers a chance to survive? Where is the government's level playing field?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that that particular company was dealing with an eroding resource, a particularly low grade of product. It could not survive based on the specie that was left.
The hon. member should also know that this 15 per cent tax which has been collected is to be used to help that particular industry. We were determined to do that, but we need help from the provincial government in order to make it work.

Mr. Speaker, this government is the eroding resource.
My supplementary is to the same minister. This government inflicted devastating measures on the forest industry and has done nothing concrete to date to change its destructive policies. This closure brings to approximately 3,000 the number jobs lost in the upper Ottawa Valley alone due to this government's policies.
When is the government going to get together with the big spenders at Queen's Park in Toronto and bring in a federal-provincial forestry agreement that will give the employers and the workers some hope for the future?

What is the government going to do for these unemployed people? Is there any mercy out there at all?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps you will allow me to answer this question. As my hon. friend knows, we have negotiated and entered into agreements with almost all provinces, now except the province of Ontario, which in itself is insisting on conducting more studies before it determines the future of the forest product sector in that province.
I would like to remind my hon. friend as well that the industry is in a normal cycle. In fact, in 1976 the Canadian dollar stood at $1,014 American and the industry survived that. There are other factors that are involved in the lack of productivity of the industry right now. One has to do with the decline in the demand of forest products in our major market, which is the United States. Current signs indicate that the recession has bottomed out and the industry will recover its vibrancy later this year.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. She will know that Soviet troops, backed by armoured vehicles and helicopters, have been storming villages along Armenia's border with Azerbaijan for the past two weeks. Earlier this month over 30 Armenians were killed and hundreds were injured when heavy fighting flared up at the border. Many Armenians suspect the Kremlin is giving support to Azerbaijan to punish Armenia for its determination to secede.
My question is: Will the minister intervene either through the United Nations or directly with the Soviets to end this anti-Armenian violence by the Soviet and Azerbaijan authorities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, clearly we are veiy concerned about the reports of increasing violence in that region, in Azerbaijan and Armenia. Like all members of the House, we regret that this conflict has not yet been resolved. We have called on all sides to show restraint in this dispute and to seek negotiated solutions because it is very important that further bloodshed be averted.
Oral Questions
I think, particularly for Canadians families of Armenian descent, there is great concern. It is up to us and we have been making representations within the Soviet Union. Our embassy has been instructed to convey our concerns directly to the Soviet Foreign Ministry and, Soviet authorities permitting, embassy officers will be making a fact-finding visit to the region so that we can report directly back to those in Canada who have an interest in this.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
Earlier in the Question Period he said he is interested in getting the fundamentals right. Well, today the Conference Board said that its "forecast for the Canadian economy,has been revised downward", and it gave as a primary reason that "export performance has been weaker than expected".
One of the fundamentals when it comes to exports is the value of the Canadian dollar. If the Minister of Finance is interested in getting the fundamentals right when it comes to exports, why is he keeping the Canadian dollar so high? Why will he not take steps to bring the value of the dollar down right now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
The hon. member knows that the exchange rate is established in the marketplace. The difficulty that Canadian industry faces is a lack of productivity and competitiveness, and that is one of the issues that needs to be addressed. The hon. member knows that there have been built up over the last two or three years serious inflationary pressures and inflationary expectations that have to be brought down. As those are brought down, interest rates are brought down. We have seen a reduction of some five percentage points in the last year.
That is the key to economic recovery. There is nothing in the Conference Board report that was not outlined in the budget of 1991 or referenced in the budget of 1990.

Mr. Speaker, one of the main factors robbing Canadian industry of its competitiveness is the over-valued Canadian dollar, and I

May 21, 1991
Oral Questions
wish that the minister would be more willing to recognize this.
The government claims to be concerned about crossborder shopping. Why will the minister not recognize that one of the fundamentals that is driving Canadians to shop in the United States is the value of the Canadian dollar? Why will he not do something about that right now if he is interested in preserving our retail industry and bringing about a strong economic recovery now and not next year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is perhaps a fundamental difference in policy. Back on August 8, 1981, his leader at that time saw no reason for an emergency session of Parliament in the face of soaring interest rates and the dropping value of the Canadian dollar, which was approaching a 50-year record low, and
12.8	per cent inflation.
Our policies are not designed to achieve that kind of a Liberal result.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture and concerns the agricultural safety net program.
Earlier this year I spoke with farmers in my constituency and I asked for their input on the type of program they would like to see implemented to see farmers through until GRIP and NISA become effective. They said: "Keep the program simple and deliver it before seeding".
NISA is now designed to allow farmers to access funds immediately in order to help pay for costs associated with seeding. The minister knows that seeding is currently under way and to date there is no indication that applications for NISA are available.
Can the minister give the farmers of my constituency an explanation as to why NISA applications are not available? And can he give some assurances as to when we can reasonably expect them to be made available?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, when the farm support adjustment measures program was announced it included the Net Income Stabilization Account and the GRIP, the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan. I can tell the hon. member that the forms for NISA, the Net Income Stabilization Account, are ready, they can be put out.
One thing my colleague should understand is that there has to be legislation passed in the provincial legislature before we would be able to send those forms out. To this point, it appears that the opposition in the Saskatchewan House is putting a political priority of its own ahead of the priority of the farmers to receive the NISA funds, which they very much would like to have as soon as possible.
Sounds NDP to me.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to inform the House of the assassination of Rajiv Gandhi earlier today during election campaigning in the state of Tamil Nadu.
Mr. Gandhi was known personally to Prime Minister Mulroney and to the former Secretary of State for External Affairs. I know that they join with me in deploring this senseless violence.
I express the profound hope of the Prime Minister and of this government that this event will not be allowed to interfere with the democratic process at this very sensitive time during this very important election to India and to those of us who have an interest in democracy and the development of democracy in India.
I know I speak for this House and for all Canadians in deploring this senseless violence and in extending condolences to the bereaved family.

Mr. Speaker, we are truly sorry to learn of Rajiv Gandhi's tragic death. We wish to extend our most sincere sympathies to the people of India and to Mr. Gandhi's family.
May 21, 1991



In a world where violence and terror has become so commonplace, it is very hard not to overlook these shocking events. Political assassinations are the most ugly of all political crimes, especially when it happens to someone who has held such a distinguished position in the largest democracy in the world.
We certainly want to share the sympathies the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have expressed, both to the family and to the people of that country.
We hope that this will not result in the further fragmentation and fracturing of that country as it goes through a very delicate and sensitive time.
We point out again the irony of human events. Once again, a member of that family has been struck down. It is a family that has provided such distinguished leadership over the years.
We hope and pray that this event will not result in further loss of life in India at this very important time.

Mr. Speaker, we certainly share the sadness at the tragedy which happened today, expressed by the minister responsible for external affairs.

Certainly, the violent death of the former Prime Minister of India affects us all and reminds us, as if it were necessary, that violence is everywhere and that democracy must triumph.

We would like to express our sadness to the family and our thoughts that democracy will triumph in India. We wish everyone in that country all the best regarding the election which is taking place. Our sincerest condolences to the family.

Mr. Speaker, I also wish to join the members of this House, on behalf of my colleagues in the Bloc Quebecois, to extend our sympathies to the Gandhi family.
Several years ago, I had the opportunity to meet the mother, who suffered the same fate as her son. We are
Privilege
all touched by events like that in one of the world's greatest democracies and we hope that this event will not be followed by an outburst of violence.
It is regrettable that democracy is thus sidetracked by violence; we bitterly regret it. Our sympathies to the family.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, notice of which was initiated by my colleague, the member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte, and which I confirmed as I was returning to the Chamber at about the time he was concluding his representation on my behalf. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for reserving for me that question of privilege.
Section 80, paragraph (2) of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fifth edition states in part:
A question of privilege-is a question partly of fact and partly of law-the law of contempt of Parliament-and is a matter for the House to determine.
I will show that the minister for immigration made an incorrect and misleading statement, which is therefore a question partly of fact.
Section 16 of Beauchesne also says:
Parliamentary privilege is the sum of the peculiar rights enjoyed by each House collectively as a constituent part of the High Court of Parliament, and by Members of each House individually, without which they could not discharge their functions -
I would like to underscore the phrase "and by Members of each House individually". Section 18 states:
-it is clear that many acts which might offend against the law or the moral sense of the community do not involve a Member's capacity to serve the people who have chosen him as their representative nor are they contrary to the usage nor derogatory to the dignity of the House of Commons.
I feel that it is contrary to the usage and derogatory to the dignity of this place when a member knowingly makes a statement that is incorrect. When such a false statement is used to assail the reputation of another hon. member the indignity to this House becomes more serious.

May 21, 1991
Privilege
Hence, when the hon. minister of immigration, in reply to my supplementary question during the proceedings of May 16, said, referring to me:
He was not even able to give me the name, the date of birth, or
address of the person we want.
This statement is on page 194 of Hansard. The minister, by his statement, impaired my ability to fully discharge my duties and obligations as a member of Parliament for Winnipeg North.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to submit the following as you consider my question of privilege:
First, with respect to the matter of the applicant's name, on May 9 I wrote a letter to the said hon. minister in which I indicated very clearly the name of the applicant visitor, Mrs. Surjit Kaur, for whom I have been making the representation. I am now prepared to table this letter if necessary. I should further inform the House that my office faxed a copy of this letter to the minister's office on the same date and the original was marked urgent and sent by messenger.
I should also inform the House that on May 13, in this Chamber, I personally approached the minister for follow-up and, once again, provided him with the name of the applicant. I am confident no member of Parliament would ever intercede for any person without knowledge of that person's name.
Second, with respect to the date of birth of the applicant visitor, my office was indeed unable to provide this information when first asked by the minister's staff, as we did not have it in our record at that time. However, on May 13 I furnished the minister's staff the date of birth, which is December 4, 1941.
I should add that the bereaved brother in Winnipeg approached the local immigration office on April 30, the day after the death of his brother, Mr. Sidhu Singh. One would assume all necessary information with respect to the applicant visitor, including the date of birth, should have been requested from the family at that time. I personally advised the minister's staff to kindly get in touch with the Winnipeg immigration office for further information.
Third, with respect to the address of the applicant, I must tell this House neither the minister's staff nor the minister himself had ever asked my staff or myself for this information, even though it has been in our case file since April 29. Certainly we would have provided this
information had it been requested. My record, Mr. Speaker, is open for your inquiry.
Thus, the minister was correct, if he meant the information on the date of birth was not initially available from my office when first requested on May 9. However, the name of the applicant has been known to us all along and to the minister's department office in Winnipeg since April 30, and to the minister's office in Ottawa since May 9, well before he requested it. I once again provided him with the information when I approached him in person on May 13.
The address of the applicant, which has been available in my record since April 29, has never been asked of me to date.
Did the minister deliberately mislead the House with the statement in question? If he did, it would be derogatory to the dignity of this House and, thus, constitute breach of privilege. Were it the case I am prepared to make the appropriate motion and seek the remedy of this House.
I realize that ministers make mistakes when they are not informed. I also realize they can make mistakes when they are wrongly or incompletely informed.
In conclusion, therefore, I would still like to believe, in all sincerity, that the minister, in reply to my question last May 16, could have mis-spoken that statement in his reply, considering the atmosphere of the moment, and that he did not deliberately and wilfully mislead the House. If this is the case, I will be prepared to accept an explanation and an apology from him and I am sure he would apologize to this House.

Mr. Speaker, in the time left, I just want to quote very briefly from the throne speech a passage which I believe to be the most important. It refers to productivity.
Increasing our productivity across the full range of Canadian industry -manufacturing, resources, and services-is the only way to secure and enhance our prosperity of the longer term. Productivity is the difference between prosperity and decline. The prosperity of all Canadians and our ability to maintain social programs depend on the productivity of Canadians. Increasing productivity requires the collaborative efforts of governments, business, labour and individual Canadians, in all regions.
I believe these are very important words. What can government do? Government can control spending, can try to balance the books and bring interest rates down.
The Address
There is no way on God's green earth that governments can borrow their way into prosperity.
To this end the government has pledged itself to legislate limits to government spending. For the first time there will be actual legislation putting a limit on government spending in this country.
In addition, legislation establishing a debt reduction fund to which the revenues from the goods and services tax and from the proceeds of privatization can be dedicated: further trade liberalization; public service reform; and privatization, where feasible. Theses are all measures designed to make the economy more competitive and to lessen the reliance upon government.
An additional measure is the pledge to work with the provinces in certain areas of education, in the elimination of interprovincial trade barriers and the management of the economy.
It is quite clear that government must control spending and inflation so that Canadians and others can have some confidence in our future.
A sound economy is the solid foundation for a strong nation. All of the hopeful signs are there: the stock market is up; interest rates are coming down; housing starts are up; business confidence is increasing; and employment opportunities are up. The path laid out in the throne speech is the best way to ensure the future: guarantee our Canadian way of life by strengthening and improving the Canadian federation constitutionally and economically.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today this debate brings us a sense of unease and frustration about the validity of the Speech from the Throne process.
In addition, I would like to focus in my intervention on what the Government of Canada says in the Speech from the Throne on the important issue of sustainable development.
May 21, 1991

Let me deal first with the Speech from the Throne as a political instrument. I would submit that at this stage the credibility, the validity and the significance of the Speech from the Throne have been lost enormously over time. I am not saying that in a partisan sense, because one can remember also speeches from the throne when my party was in power which were not fully implemented. In other words, it is a statement of dreams, a statement of intent. However, it is a statement that because of its lack of accountability at the present time has to be questioned.
We know that Canadians at large at this particular time in history have raised questions about the credibility of the political system. Therefore, I submit that it is necessary and incumbent upon us to raise a question of this kind with you, Mr. Speaker, because it is valid, it is timely and it is necessary.
I will illustrate this point with a few examples to move from the abstract, so to speak, into the practical.
Why am I saying that the Speech from the Throne reduces even further the credibility of politicians? I would ask you to compare the Speech from the Throne of April 1989, in which you will find under the heading "Environmental Imperative" a number of specific proposals. I will start with the one which reads: "The government has also altered its operational practices and enlarged the responsibilities of the Minister of the Environment to ensure that environmental issues are fully considered in the course of its decision making".
That was a very bold, a very promising and a very welcome statement two years ago. If we look at what happened, without reciting a number of events that have proven the contrary, I would only ask you to think back to last week when the courts made a decision on Kemano II and urged that the government apply its own environmental impact assessment process.
This was a decision, is a decision and will be a decision of enormous importance. In other words, the court told the federal government that it was breaking its own environmental impact assessment rules. This was last week, and by comparing that event with what was in the Speech from the Throne two years ago, one cannot help but conclude that something here has gone seriously wrong.
The Address
I would submit that the gap between the rhetoric in the pages and lines of a Speech from the Throne and the action is widening in a dangerous manner.
If you look at the 1989 Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, you will find a statement to the effect that in [DOT]the new environmental agenda the government will limit the environmental impact of toxic chemicals through the development of regulations for the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
As of today, under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act no new chemicals have been added since the birth of this legislation. Before this legislation came into effect nine chemicals were included, precisely nine out of thousands and thousands of chemicals that were in use out there, and today we still have nine. Therefore, the inevitable question is: What has happened to this important commitment?
Let me move to another example. In April 1989, the government committed itself to improving the quality of our water through new legislation. Nothing has happened since. We had the Pierce report on the federal water inquiry in 1985. We had the publication of a federal water policy in 1987. We had a commitment from the government in April 1989, and we are still waiting for the legislation.
If you want another example, there was a very important policy commitment in April 1989 to protect the environmental integrity of our Arctic regions. What do we find here? We find that a few days before the last session died an Arctic strategy was released. It is another piece of paper; it is not an implementation of an Arctic protection strategy.
I must bring the strategy itself to your attention, Mr. Speaker, because you come from a province which is undertaking or proposing a major hydroelectric plant that could affect the salinity in Hudson Bay. I come from a province where eventually over the decades similar projects will be proposed, with an impact on James Bay, which is part of Hudson Bay. Manitoba is also in the long term likely to produce some hydroelectric plans of that nature.
In the Arctic strategy there is no reference to the importance of the ecological role of Hudson Bay, its salinity, or how it could be affected by these megaprojects as they are being proposed to come on stream.

May 21, 1991
The Address
What we have instead of protection are nice words, beautiful sentences and lots of paper.
In the April 1989 Speech from the Throne, there is a reference which reads: "My government will proceed with the initiatives to clean up the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River and, together with the provinces, to further the process of cleaning up dangerous land sites".
The remedial action plan for 17 Canadian sites in the Great Lakes and in the St. Lawrence River lacks federal support. We have not seen the action that was proposed in the Speech from the Throne two years ago.
The Speech from the Throne of two years ago proposed the encouragement, the development and the adoption of clean and efficient production processes.
We have a situation where, unfortunately, we cannot say that this has happened. In our tax system, the only write-offs refer to pollution control equipment, a narrow range of devices related to equipment. Clean production processes that aim as close as possible to zero discharge do not qualify yet for tax breaks.
In other words, the government, despite the intent that it expressed two years ago, has not yet been able to come to grips with the use of fiscal and taxation levers and instruments that would allow it to implement what it promised to do two years ago.
We have the commitment by the government, also two years ago, to legislation that would ensure an appropriate environmental assessment review process.
On that, the government attempted to act. In June 1990, it introduced Bill C-78, which did not make any progress during the summer of last year. Between January and April, it was no longer the object of discussions in committee.
In addition to that, it was quite interesting to notice that witnesses who came before the committee on that environmental impact assessment bill were of the opinion that they would prefer to live under the present guidelines than under the weaker and vague clauses that are embodied in the now defunct Bill C-78.
Might I add that the guidelines are the result of an Order in Council decision by the then Liberal government in the spring of 1984.
We have a situation where we are still living in a legislative vacuum, but instead of legislation we have a stronger regime thanks to guidelines that are in place by way of a decision of the courts.
In the Speech from the Throne of two years ago, and before I move on to sustainable development, there was also a commitment by the government to a national child care program.
Inevitably, one has to ask, if one were an average Canadian looking at the Speech from the Throne of two years ago, what happened to that commitment. Unfortunately, we cannot find any initiatives, not even the shadow of a bill in the legislative system, that would indicate that the commitment has somehow been developed and given the necessary political will to move ahead into the legislative system.
Actually, it is not only on the child care program front that we find the Speech from the Throne wanting. It is not only wanting because of what was not implemented since 1989 in the previous Speech from the Throne.
We find an absence of understanding of the social agenda of Canadians at large, the situation being faced by one-parent families, the situation being faced by people who depend on food banks, the situation of people who are waiting to be admitted to social housing, the situation of those who are unemployed and are waiting to be recalled to their job or perhaps are not going to be recalled at all because their previous job has simply disappeared.
The absence of social awareness and conscience in this particular Speech from the Throne is particularly striking and particularly shocking.
I indicated a few minutes ago that the second reason for making this intervention relates to the issue of sustainable development. I must refer you to the present Speech from the Throne. I was astounded to read the following statement under the heading "Participating in Prosperity":
My government will, over the coming months, consult with provincial governments, industry and environmental leaders to explore means of complementing current regulatory approaches with innovative instruments that would achieve positive environmental results-
May 21, 1991

And here are the key words, Mr. Speaker, before you fall asleep:
-without prejudicing economic prosperity.
That really struck me like a thunderbolt. By saying "without prejudicing economic prosperity" the Government of Canada rejects all the commitments it has made so far to sustainable development and the commitments made so far, including the Speech from the Throne of 1989, to the Brundtland report and our common future.
The government is saying that the environment will only count if the economy does not come into the picture, which is diametrically opposed to the principles and recommendations contained in the Brundtland report. This is contrary to what sustainable development is all about because sustainable development means development that can be sustained over a long period of time without prejudicing the choices and opportunities of generations to come.
You can invent another dozen definitions if you like, if you have enough imagination.
The point I am trying to make is that this government, either out of bad faith when it was popular decided to embrace sustainable development hoping that it could ride the popularity of that concept and maintain public support and possibly increase it, or embraced it without knowing what it was embracing, without realizing what sustainable development meant.
This is a government that either attempted to deceive the public or was stupid enough to embrace a concept whose meaning it did not understand. The proof of that was a few weeks ago during Question Period in this Elouse when the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, now minister in charge of federal-provincial relations, in reply to a question from the member for Skeena, insisted that the trade negotiations and the environmental negotiations presently taking place between the United States and Mexico, and eventually involving Canada, would have to proceed on separate tracks. At that point we knew that conceptually this government was unable to understand the significance of what sustainable development is all about.
Therefore, and it was almost prophetic in a sense, the reply given by the secretary of state, that revelation, has
The Address
found its way into the text of the Speech from the Throne. When the government says it will introduce innovative instruments to achieve positive environmental results without prejudicing economic prosperity, it is saying that it has chosen a policy that will take care of the short term, that it will endanger our natural resources and that it will perpetrate the mistakes that have been made in the environment and in environmental policies over several decades, particularly in recent years.
In other words, it is saying that political expediency will come before long-term benefits. It is saying that it endorses particularly in international bodies, in the United Nations and at conferences on climate change, certain principles and concepts in the world community but it does not want to practise them at home. It is saying it has decided that the integration of economic and environmental goals is not a knock on the table. It is attempting to turn the clock back 20 years. What a shame, what a disgrace for the Canadian people.
