Mr. Speaker, through you to the member, there was an article in the New York Times yesterday by an American environmentalist who argued-the member probably saw it- that because President Bush had agreed to factor the environment into the talks that somehow the environment in effect was likely to be safe.
If the member saw the article, I wonder if he would wish to comment on that principle.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. I have not seen that article but I am aware of the theology being adopted by the administration in Washington which has unfortunately been swallowed hook, line and sinker by the administration here in Ottawa, as demonstrated by the endorsement given almost overnight by the Minister for International Trade of the approach that the hon. member just attributed to President Bush.
There is a lot of environment in trade policies because there are very few other human activities that impinge so heavily on environment and our national resources as trade activities in any jurisdiction. To pretend out of the blue that trade policies have to be considered on one track and then on another track you should consider

May 21, 1991
The Address
environmental policies is an unreal conceptual organization.
If I remember correctly, the administration in Washington went so far as to say that the two would be considered on parallel tracks: trade on one track and the environment on the other. Anyone who knows geometry knows that parallel lines never meet. That fact alone reveals the weakness of this particular approach. A separation of the two will not allow an examination of trade activities with the environment in mind with a concern for the long term. It will not allow a concern for the capacity of natural resources to rejuvenate themselves while anticipating and preventing pollution activities resulting from trade. In other words, one cannot have a meaningful trade negotiation process at the table without having people knowledgeable on the environment as part of that particular trade delegation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, first of all, the start of a new session in the life of this Thirty-Fourth Parliament is a proper occasion to thoughtfully and carefully reflect on our collective achievements, as a Parliament and people. It is also a time to provide both leadership and vision for the long-term future of our nation.
No issue is more important, as stated in the Speech from the Throne, than the unity of Canada. We must learn to overcome obstacles, erase doubts, and strengthen Canada's position to meet the challenges of the twenty-first century which is waiting for us just around the comer.
All hon. members are united in this purpose, as far as I know, and the government's commitment to Canada and to our vision for the future is strong and clear in this Speach from the Throne. If, in our minds, the picture of the future is dim and clouded, and if we remain preoccupied only with the whims and pressures of today, we put at risk our very future.
Daily, we face such constant pressures and exhortations. However, to deal only with today and let the future take care of itself, spend a few billion here and there, invent a new program overnight to demonstrate concern and action, not worry about the national debt, not question the value of existing programs, and not even wonder if a new costly effort is certain to be cost
effective and bring the desired results, is a dangerous and costly attitude.
Keeping our eye firmly on the long-term and staying the course is difficult for some hon. members. Satisfying every want and wish today comes just too naturally. It may play well to the cameras.
However it does not meet our duty and responsibility as Parliamentarians. As members of this House, we must resist the temptation of pressing for instant gratification and magic solutions for every real or imagined need. Magic wands such as popular but ineffective policies are hoaxes. They don't work.
What does work is implementing today carefully-designed measures directed to achieving long-term goals. As I said earlier, the year 2000 is not far off and our focus on the future must not prevent immediate action. This action must be in line with goals for the future. This is the view, and the vision, that is put forward to this House and the people of Canada in the speech from the Throne.
This has been the guiding principle of this Government since 1984. The foundation has been the Strategy for Economic Renewal: We have firmly put the break on the mindless expansion of government programs and expenditures; deficit reduction has been and remains a primary goal; tax reform is yielding economic returns; and free trade and productivity growth open the doors to prosperity and the world for all Canadians.
There is no other route for making it in the tough competitive world we face. Let us not deceive Canadians into believing otherwise. Wise leadership and effective management is our mandate. That demands that we confront directly the complex challenges and problems facing Canadians.
Moreover, that means developing coherent and consistent long-term plans to meet goals and targets and stick to them.
It also means taking the time and devoting the energy to build a concensus among Canadians. Broad agreement among Canadians does not simply arise on command to suit the agenda or meet the demands of those who call for instant solutions. Such a consensus must be encouraged and nurtured in a deliberate and planned way. Leaders must make the commitment and set the course. Knowledge and power has to be shared. New
May 21, 1991

forums and meeting places need to be fashioned. Energy and time must be invested.
To pretend that we have all the answers and reject the need for public consultations-and those critical requirements to make consultation work-is to mislead Canadians.

It is not government but people who have the real power in our society to set the course and make the rules which govern their lives. Certain people in this Chamber question or even ridicule the government's decision to consult seriously and widely with the Canadian people.
The people who are questioning or ridiculing a commitment like this one by the government are, in reality, questioning and ridiculing a commitment to empower people and make democracy work.
As the Speech from the Throne clearly states, increasing prosperity is first and foremost an issue of people. Canada is much more than an abundance of forests, minerals and water. Our greatest strength is our people. Our knowledge, skills and brains are our greatest national asset. They are our ticket to prosperity and they are our ticket to growth, more so than they have ever been in the past.
This is a tough and competitive world that values knowledge more than any other asset. Canadian jobs are being threatened by a new kind of competition. It is not primarily low wage competition that threatens us, increasingly it is high wage competition. Canada is losing ground to industrial competitors who are simply better than we are at inventing, designing, managing, manufacturing and marketing. We must, and we can, outsmart our international competitors.
In this, the information society, the knowledge age, how well we live will depend on how well we learn. Learning, from infancy, in school, on the job, and throughout life.
Governments in Canada spend more than $50 billion a year on education and training, with federal expenditures amounting to over $11 billion. This is a greater expenditure than almost any other developed country in the world, but the results, not government spending
The Address
more money, is the question that should be of most concern to every Canadian.
The importance of learning as our ticket to prosperity is not a new concern for us. The Prime Minister has strongly asserted, over the years, the national interest in calling for all Canadians, all levels of government and all groups in society to recognize and then confront the fact that our performance lags behind other developed nations.
Our government, under the Prime Minister's strong direction, has established a record of important accomplishments to further learning, amounting to billions of dollars in expenditures. This represents an innovative and creative record. Each initiative is targeted to deal with the specific issue. Together they represent an integrated approach.
These new measures, many in my own Department of Employment and Immigration, include the new Labour Force Development Strategy, the National Stay-inSchool Initiative, Canada scholarships from Industry, Science and Technology, major literacy initiatives, networks of Centres of Excellence, Canada Student Loans Policy Review, education for Canada's First Nations, the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy and the Aboriginal Employment and Training Strategy.
In November 1989 at the First Ministers' Conference, the Prime Minister defined the challenge and provided the leadership. There was wide recognition and understanding then, as there must be today, that learning throughout life, good jobs and our success as a nation are closely linked.
Who in Canada wants low paying and low skill jobs? No one wishes such a future for themselves or their children. The ticket to good jobs and a good life throughout one's life is learning. The ultimate goal which can be shared by all Canadians and all levels of government is to build an innovative, competitive economy, based on high skill, high wage jobs, a society where all Canadians value learning and fully enjoy the benefits of their learning and labour.
Learning reform is rooted in international competitiveness and is a function of national economic policy. The European commission and the sovereign member nations are forging ahead in developing European-wide targets and standards.

May 21, 1991
The Address
The Americans, the Japanese and other developed nations are confronting this challenge more successfully than Canadians.

Compared to many of these other countries, Mr. Speaker, our human resources are underdeveloped and underutilized. The fundamental problem with learning in Canada is that, compared with other nations, there isn't enough of it, and we don't take it seriously enough. Our prosperity depends on major improvements in the general level of skills held by all, as well as having many more people with advanced and specialized skills. No one party has a monopoly on life-long learning. The provinces have undisputed primacy for schools, a pat recognized in the speech from the Throne. We fully respect the Provinces' jurisdiction. The federal government has long played a major role in adult training. Life-long learning requires that we all work in partnership to confront our competitors.
Future constitutional restructuring in this area is not ruled out. In fact it could be informed by wide consultation. What is proposed in the speech from the Throne is a call for a national consensus on performance, goals, partnerships, and priorities for learning.
To build this consensus, we will now launch a process of consultation throughout Canada. This will represent another major step to further learning. It will focus the attention of all on the benefits of developing a learning culture in Canada.

A commitment has been made to publish a discussion paper on learning. This paper, now in draft form, has been prepared under the close direction of the Prime Minister. It fully reflects his long-standing commitment to learning, to further Canada's competitiveness, and to provide greater prosperity and personal fulfilment for each individual Canadian. This paper will be the federal government's contribution to a national dialogue on how Canadians acquire their skills and knowledge and how our approach to learning can be improved to ensure that Canadians can continue to enjoy the benefits of a globally competitive economy in the 21st century.
The primary aim of the paper is to initiate a national consensus-building discussion on targets and priorities for learning in Canada. While we have some understanding of the extent of the problem and the challenge we
face as a nation, change will not happen unless public attitudes change.
This is the core of what we seek to accomplish, creating a climate or a culture among individuals, employers and all others to both learn throughout life and increase wide demand for better, if not outstanding, performance.
Change will only occur when large numbers of Canadians of all ages choose to make learning a personal priority and an individual responsibility throughout life. Learning is not something done to us by external institutions. Learning is what we can choose to do or not. The enormous personal, spiritual and economic benefits that learning can produce for each individual can be defined and readily understood. They can be a major source of new wealth for eveiy Canadian.
These benefits must be made widely known. This revelation alone could be the spark that ignites an interest in more Canadians to pursue a life of learning and personal growth, and to create demand and support further reform.

Four Canada-wide goals for the year 2000 are suggested in the Speech from the Throne. With Provincial endorsement and cooperation, these could be considered by Canadians: cutting illiteracy rates in half; ensuring that 90 per cent of Canadians graduate from high school or the equivalent; doubling the number of post-seconda-ly graduates in mathematics, the sciences, and engineering; and quadrupling the training provided by employers to their empoyees.
Mr. Speaker, there are many other goals that Canadians can consider in defining a learning system for life that is among the best, if not the best, in the world. Today, I might suggest two more goals that Canadians could discuss, namely to double the number of Canadian youth who participate in a structured learning programs leading to entry-level jobs and to achieve full representation of women in the fields of mathematics, science and technology.
These, and many other goals, will be suggested and examined in the discussion paper. As the Minister responsible, I can inform Members to day that the discussion paper will be tabled in the House within
May 21, 1991

several weeks. I will be a substantial and important contribution to our knowledge.
The release of this paper will be a first step in a process of consultation and consensus building with Canadians throughout the nation.

In the several weeks following the release of the paper I will be meeting with many across Canada to decide on the approach to the process of consultation. Public consultations should start within the coming several months and throughout we want to examine learning as a life-long activity and the reforms required.
I will keep hon. members of this House fully informed and seek their views and support at every stage. Members from all sides of this House have indicated on many occasions support and commitment to the goal of improving our performance and furthering learning for all Canadians. We share the recognition that this is one of the most important challenges facing Canada. We have as a nation one of the strongest, best staffed and amply funded education systems. If together we deliberately build on our intellectual strengths we can take on the world. We will become competitive with the best learning systems in the world and create prosperity for ourselves as we enrich our own personal lives.

Our increased prosperity will help to build the unity of Canada. Not for today alone, but for the long term.

Mr. Speaker, there are many things in this throne speech which make the people of Canada question this government's commitment to the improvement of the quality of life for Canadians.
A considerable amount of time has been spent in the last few days considering the pros and cons of the plan of action as it was presented in the Speech from the Throne and on the main issues raised in this plan of action, important issues such as competition, unity, prosperity, education, and parliamentary reform.
However, I want to look at some of the things that were not mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. The quality of a civilization is judged by its treatment of the elderly, the children, and those in need, the so-called underprivileged. We cannot in this modern world ignore the lame, the weak, and the hungry in other parts of the world while we take care of ourselves here at home.
In the Speech from the Throne the government has ignored its responsibility for the needs of the so-called Third World. In fact there is no mention of the hungry world. There is no mention of the need for development. There is no mention of our responsibility in these areas.
The speech came close to this issue once. It said:
Last September, at the Children's Summit in New York, the attention of people everywhere was focused on children at risk. Seventy-one leaders pledged that that moment would last a decade.
Our Prime Minister promised a decade of assistance to children in need. That implied assistance to the world's children. However, the next line of this particular quotation from the Speech from the Throne indicated that the government was somewhat introverted in this particular area because it went on to say:
My government will bring forward a plan to implement the commitments it made that day: the objectives to see Canadian girls and boys better educated, better protected and better nurtured so that they can make their own contributions to Canada's future.
In other words, even as we made a commitment to the world in this Speech from the Throne, we turned it back on ourselves. There was no suggestion that the Prime Minister would continue the leadership he indicated in
that conference, that his promises at that time would be honoured.
In this speech there is no mention of how we will do our share in taking care of the world's destitute.
Along with the slashing of foreign aid spending in the February 25 budget by more than $5 billion over the next five years, this lack of mention in the Speech from the Throne indicates, or at least leaves the perception, that Canada is withdrawing from its involvement in humanitarian aid to those countries needing it most.
Right now is the time for Canada to be aggressive in our leadership in humanitarian aid, aggressive in our involvement with development of Third World countries.
Right now around the world, one billion people live in absolute poverty. One billion adults can neither read nor write. One hundred eighty million children suffer from malnutrition, that is Canada's population multiplied by about six. Three million children die each year from diseases against which they can be immunized. These are the year to year statistics.
Right now we have a special outstanding requirement in places like the Horn of Africa. In the Sudan, it is expected that 300,000 people will die of starvation in the next few weeks, even if immediate food aid is sent into that area. If that aid is delayed, the number of people who will die will increase proportionately to the days and weeks it is delayed.
In Ethiopia, the war situation has brought the food movement to a halt, temporarily we hope. Up to 7 million people are in danger.
In Somalia, there is a mass movement of millions because of food shortages. They are moving from one food shortage area to another. So little organization is available in that particular country that no one knows what can be done or what needs to be done.
I do not expect that Canada can jump in and solve all these situations, nor does the world expect Canada to do it. However, we should not ignore it or even seem to ignore it, which is what the Speech from the Throne does.
Granted there are many problems in the Third World, problems which seem to suggest that we are just wasting good money by giving aid. There is excessive spending in the military. There is wasteful public spending of other types. There are unnecessary projects which are taking a considerable amount of money. There is corruption.
May 21, 1991

There is abusive lending on the part of organizations such as the World Bank and the IMF, which are part of the donor structure. There is trade that undermines the production of the people and, in many cases, the health of the people.
The UN, in a report that was released just a few days ago, suggests that Africa, which has become the continent most in need of aid, receives more than $6 billion in so-called technical assistance. However, too much is spent on foreign experts and too little on building up local institutions and national consultants.
This aid does not reduce the need for humanitarian aid, nor does it mean that Canada should wait for these improvements. The starvation and death statistics will not go away without action. That action is expected of Canada and Canada has to take leadership and give continued aid. We cannot just ignore the problem.
The Speech from the Throne suggests massive increases in spending on education, and that is commendable. If it happens, it should be a continued policy of our government. The government's record of cutting assistance to education does not give us too much hope in that particular area.
However, it ignores the world's need for literacy training. In the Niger only 15 per cent of its adult population is literate, in the Sudan only 23 per cent of its population is literate. So, even as we hope for better education for Canadians, we cannot forget the rest of the world.
Why do I dwell on the Third World when the Speech from the Throne talks about what is happening in Canada? I talk about the Third World because, as we are told daily by this government, we are a global society. Our prosperity, a throne speech theme by the way, is dependent on our ability to be competitive in the world.
Sometimes it appears that this competitiveness must always be at the expense of some other country. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate in response to the Speech from the Throne and would like to divide my comments into two parts: the first dealing with the economic side of the Throne Speech and the second with constitutional renewal and the national unity question.
Canada has one of the highest standards of living in the world and a quality of life that is the envy of almost every nation. However there is no guarantee this prosperity will continue. Simply relying on things that have helped us succeed in the past will not be enough to improve our material welfare and quality of life in the future.
Therefore, I am pleased that the Speech from the Throne addressed the very important topic of restoring economic competitiveness to Canadian industry.
During the past four-week break from Parliament I spoke with some 60 company presidents and many of their employees in my riding. The message they all gave me was unanimous: Canadians must work more effectively together in a partnership of management and labour to meet Canada's competitive challenges over the next several years. We absolutely must become more productive and competitive.
Mr. Speaker, you will notice that I purposely left the government out of that bilateral partnership between management and labour, because the role of government is to set up a free and open economic environment, set ground rules for that competition and working environment, lay down the tax structure and rules for investment and then step aside and allow both labour and management to create economic wealth and prosperity.
Our budget of February 26 of this year reinforced our commitment to restore the economic health of this country. We have made considerable progress to date even though our efforts have been roundly opposed, ridiculed and condemned. Canadians have not taken kindly to suddenly being deprived of the many gifts and handouts of the irresponsible federal government of the Trudeau Liberal era from 1968 to 1984, during which time we saw the damaging fiscal policies that created a near bankrupt position.
Now, unfortunately, these same policies are about to be repeated by Ontario's NDP government. While Ontario will double its debt load in the next four years to a deficit which took 124 years to accumulate, we at the federal level are legislating a mandatory program of 3 per cent spending limits.
Second, we are establishing a debt servicing and reduction fund solely dedicated to offsetting the costs of the public debt. By law, net revenues from the GST and from privatization will flow into this fund.
With regard to enhanced competitiveness and productivity, we are making some progress since, for the first time in 16 years, we have been attracting more direct investment into Canada than has been going abroad.
In 1984, direct investment outflows were over $11 billion. Progressively and incrementally since 1984, investment outflows have grown smaller and smaller. Now we have turned it around.
Currently we are experiencing a positive direct investment inflow of approximately $500 million. Contrary to popular perceptions, according to Statistics Canada, exports from most industries to the United States since the implementation of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement have risen.
For example, after two years of the 10-year phase-in period of the agreement, sectors such as food and beverages, rubber and plastics, textiles, clothing, furniture, transportation and electrical products have experienced increases in exports ranging from the low 20 per cent to as high as 67 per cent.
Now we are entering into discussions with the United States and Mexico regarding a North American free

trade agreement. We did not ask for this. Mexico did, but there is no way that we could stand idly by while two other nations, our neighbours, negotiate such an agreement. We must participate in the talks if for no other reason than to protect our interests and the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
Furthermore, this opportunity can be used for Canada's long-term gain in the larger North American free trade zone. I am convinced that this possibility will be beneficial to Canada in the long run, especially in the light of changing global trading realities.
As a representative of a manufacturing constituency in southwestern Ontario, the federal riding of Kitchener, I agree with the Simon Fraser University economist, Dr. Richard Lipsey, who has often appeared before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade on trade related matters, that we might consider a 20-year rather than a 10-year phase-in of the agreement for certain industrial and other sectors due to a variety of reasons and differences between Canada and Mexico that are not the case between Canada and the United States.
Before commenting on the second issue of national unity, I would like to add that I am pleased with the sentence in the throne speech which reads: "My government will review its policies in relation to the family, the most fundamental building block of Canadian society."
I hope that this will result in more favourable taxation treatment for the traditional family. I also hope that we will bring in provisions that will make it easier for younger families to acquire a home that they can actually enjoy.
I know that lower interest rates will help tremendously in this direction, but I think we also have to look creatively at other means which would assist that.
Further, I would like to see a tough pornography bill that would protect our children and women from degrading and disgusting violent forms of pornography, which are far too easily accessible in Canada today and which treat our children and women as things and not as human beings.
The second theme of the Speech from the Throne was Canadian unity.
The Address
Much has been attempted to ensure the unity and strengthening of our Confederation. Recently, the Meech Lake round almost succeeded where the constitutional amendments of the early 1980s had failed, that is including the province of Quebec as a signatory to these changes.
Presently, two commissions have tabled their studies in the province of Quebec. Additionally, the Beaudoin-Ed-wards study of Canada's amending formula and the Spicer Commission on Canadian values, attitudes and aspirations are to report by July 1.
Other provinces will soon be receiving their own constitutional studies. The Speech from the Throne announced the creation of another special joint parliamentary committee to bring together the recommendations of these many studies. It will also be given the mandate to meet with provincial legislators and aboriginal groups and to report back by February 1992.
As a result of these many studies and consultations, the federal government will propose its plan for a renewed Canada. Some have said "oh, no, not another committee." However, given the severity of the issue and the attitude of so many Canadians that Meech Lake was developed in secrecy, it is far better to err on the side of yet another open consultation than risk the loss of making real progress, thereby creating the misunderstanding and mistrust of earlier attempts.
It is my hope that when we discuss the issue of national unity, we do so in the spirit of tolerance, compromise and non-partisan debate.
We now need to state what a former president of the United States once said: "Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country." John Kennedy took those words from the French philosopher, Rousseau, who wrote: "As soon as any man says of the affairs of state, 'What does it matter to me?' that state may be given up as lost."
All Canadians must stop thinking pessimistically about Canada today and I would recommend that all would cease all talk of separation and all debate of "let them go" or "good riddance to them" because to me, a Canada without Quebec is no Canada at all.

May 21, 1991
The Address
Let us each dedicate ourselves as Canadians, and each of us as members of the only democratically elected, accountable and true constituent assembly of Canada, the House of Commons, to now work together in healing our great land to preserve its unity and strength for ourselves and our children.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to the member's observations about the fiscal policy being pursued by the Conservative government. He had some criticism directed toward the previous Liberal government which is consistent with what we hear from members of his party. It has now been almost seven years since the Conservative government took office and rather than standing up and accepting responsibility for the affairs of state, it is still talking about what happened eight, nine years ago, and is still blaming its predecessor for the ills of the country.
I find it really astonishing that members of that party would not stand up and accept the responsibility. I would like to draw to the hon. member's attention the fact that the former Minister of Finance in his first budget six years ago said that he would get the deficit down to $18 billion by the end of the decade. That is, presumably, by December 31, 1990.
In his last budget several months ago, the former Minister of Finance predicted a deficit of $30.5 billion for the fiscal year-I believe it is-ending March 31. He missed the mark by the small sum of some $12.5 billion and yet we have members like the one who just spoke, who have the nerve to stand up in this House and give us lectures about fiscal discipline.
I would ask the member to be a bit more humble when it comes to talking about the accomplishments of his government.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member is saying that this government has now been in office approaching its seventh year and is asking when is it going to take responsibility for some of what it is doing.
We are pleased to take responsibility for our actions. We have turned around a generation of going in the
wrong direction, and you cannot do that overnight. We have brought in some very significant changes.
The members in the Liberal Party like to suggest that we have doubled the national debt. What they forget to say is that in our first three years of operation, we took the national accounts of all the revenues received that go out for programs spending, and we took a deficit of $16 billion and we moved it to $8 billion, then to $2 billion, and for the last four years we have been operating on a surplus. Were it not for interest and compound interest on the national debt left to us by the party of the member who asked the question, we would now have a surplus, we would have balanced budgets.
What the hon. member is ignoring is that for the last four years of the seven, this government has not added one single penny to the national debt; all that has been happening is compound interest on the national debt.
The hon. member made his point and said he would like a little humility from us. It is taking longer than we had hoped, that is true, but the severity of the problem that was left to us in the compound interest factor is huge and immense and we are working at that.
Look at the legacy of spending in the previous 16 years that created this question compared to the legacy of spending now for the past seven years. Look at the average spending of over 10 per cent in the previous 10 years, compared to the now 3.7. We are now bringing in a legislated ceiling of 3 per cent on spending. We are coming to grips with the issue. We are making some success, and if we can continue in the direction we are heading we can see the end of the problem. Should they ever come back, we would see a bankrupt nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It gives me great pleasure to take part in this debate. This Speech from the Throne touches on several of the priorities that the government has identified for the upcoming session. I believe that this Speech from the Throne identifies many of the priorities on the agenda of Canadians.
What are these issues that Canadians have identified? Canadians are interested in the future of Canada; they are interested in the future that they are going to build for themselves and for their children. They want to know about jobs; they want to know that the government has a
May 21, 1991

definite plan to address the economic problems that block the paths to prosperity.
Canadians know that this government has this plan. For too long they have seen spendthrift governments borrow from our children's future to pay for questionable excesses. That changed in 1984. Although the ability of this government to serve Canadians has been limited by the burden of debt left to us by the previous government, the last budget has shown us that there is light at the end of the debt tunnel.
Canadians signalled their desire for change in 1984 and they reaffirmed that desire in 1988. The reason for this is simple: Canada was in a mess that would only get worse unless a measure of reason could be restored to the way the government operated.
We have gone far to restore that reason, and this Speech from the Throne indicates that we are willing and able to go the distance in providing Canadians with the kind of government that they need and want.
The over-all message that comes from this Speech from the Throne is that it is time for us, for all Canadians, to re-examine our attitudes. Before we can see ourselves reflected in the Constitution, we must know who we are; we need to know more about our history. It is time to search our souls and it is time for us to learn about ourselves and to rediscover the real priorities in life.
I am encouraged by the government's reaffirmation that the family is the most fundamental building block of Canadian society.
This is a very significant approach to the troubles facing Canada today. A strong sense of family leads to a strong sense of self. This strong sense of self brings with it the confidence and initiative that results in a productive and prosperous society, a society free from insecurity-
For too long Canada has suffered from insecurity. We have been without the focus and the sense of purpose that comes from a sound knowledge of self. I believe that if we can strengthen the family, we will strengthen society.
In reviewing its policies toward the family, I believe that it is necessary to restore fairness to the taxation system so that Canadians who choose to be a traditional family are not disadvantaged.
The Address
The Department of Finance will have to look closely at the existing system and find ways to provide fairness for all Canadians, including traditional families.
The government has indicated that it will be bringing forward initiatives to ensure the protection of children within our society. One of the many ways that the government can do this is by strengthening the family unit.
Before I continue, I would like to take a moment to pay tribute to the men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces. We have just seen the Canadian Armed Forces participate in a world effort to settle the crisis in the Persian Gulf. This participation is cause for great pride. Canada's role in the crisis has drawn Canadians together. It has been a unifying force. Canada has been, and continues to be, well served by the men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces.
In my riding of Fraser Valley East we have Canadian Forces Base Chilliwack. This is the only Canadian Forces Base on mainland British Columbia. It is the proud home of the 1st Combat Engineer Regiment. A major portion of the 1st Combat Engineer Regiment is now on duty in Kuwait doing demolition work, clearing mine fields. These some 300 Canadians are proving with their actions that the training that occurs at the engineering school at CFB Chilliwack is invaluable.
CFB Chilliwack is more than just the home of the 1st Combat Engineer Regiment. There is the school of military engineering and there is also the officer's candidate training school. CFB Chilliwack is also the logistic centre for the militia in mainland British Columbia. It is the only base in Canada where the heavy equipment training can go on year round. It is minutes from secluded and isolated training areas and minutes from urban areas.
British Columbia is a unique part of Canada and CFB Chilliwack is a unique Canadian institution. Without CFB Chilliwack, B.C. would be without a Canadian Armed Forces presence on the mainland. An Armed forces presence is essential. It is essential to note that there are a number of federal correctional institutions within a 30-minute radius of CFB Chilliwack.
During the Matsqui Institute riots in 1970, the forces were called upon to provide assistance and restore order. The significance of this resource should not escape us.

May 21, 1991
The Address
Disaster preparedness is also a consideration, especially considering the geography of B.C.
We, in B.C. and in the Fraser Valley, are well aware of the important role that CFB Chilliwack plays. The base is a unifying element. Rumours that the base may be closed have caused us great concern. After the remarkable role the Canadian forces played and continue to play in the Persian Gulf, and bearing in mind the pride that Canadians felt because of that participation, a very unifying pride I might add, I say let us keep our priorities straight.
CFB Chilliwack is an integral part of the Canadian Armed Forces and an integral part of the community. It is the forces' presence on the mainland in British Columbia and is not a base that can be considered eligible for closing. In 1992 Canada celebrates its 125th birthday; Montreal celebrates its 400th; Matsqui, its 100th birthday. CFB Chilliwack will celebrate its 50th anniversary. I hope that we will be able to mark the four celebrations together.
The Speech from the Throne mentions that we must proceed with caution as we enter into a new stage of constitutional building. What we must do is change our attitude as a society. In addition to strengthening the family unit, we must look at our relationship to the institutions of government. We hear a great deal about rights, but we do not hear a lot about responsibilities.
In congratulating new Canadians upon receiving citizenship, I often take a moment to remind them that with the rights and privileges of Canadian citizenship come many responsibilities. I tell them that Canada has become the great country that it is because people have recognized that as citizens they have a responsibility to take part and become involved in our society. As citizens, we define what Canadian society is.
A country like Canada is always changing. It is like a person who is growing up and going through a maturing process. All Canadian citizens, whether they are born here or choose to come here, help Canada to mature and grow. For Canada to be the best that it can possibly be, everyone must take part and contribute. This is the
responsibility. This is the flip side to the rights and privileges.
We must remember our heritage, but we cannot be limited by that heritage. When we share our personal heritage and culture with each other, we create a better society. When we build barriers, we miss out on the benefits of sharing. Instead, we see ignorance and hostility. It is this ignorance and hostility that leads to disunity and talk of separation. This causes me great concern.
My parents were bom in Shawville, Quebec. They homesteaded in southern Saskatchewan and farmed there for some 60-odd years. I grew up on the prairies and having moved to British Columbia, chose to raise my family there. I am proud to be a Canadian and have my roots throughout the country. I am proud to share my heritage with other Canadians who come from other parts of the country and who have come from other parts of the world.
The energy and resources that we expend trying to convince ourselves that we have a country worth having is astounding. I look around me and see what we have in Canada and can only shake my head in wonder. We are the envy of the world.
Yet, the problem of disunity in this country is very serious. If we can once get beyond this issue, we can raise the level of debate in this country and can raise the standard of living. We can re-channel the enormous resources now spent on trying to solve our problems toward creating a better standard of living for our children. Now is the time to act, and we must. We cannot listen to the voices that represent only parts of our country, the voices that would have this country tom apart, the voices that would build barriers to understanding. Instead of encouraging Canadians from all parts of Canada to get to know one another, these parties would have us turn our backs and create new solitudes.
I am encouraged by the Speech from the Throne. The government is committed to unifying the country. By strengthening the family, the fundamental building block of society, the government will ensure that Canada will enter the 21st century in sound shape. These are important times in the life of our nation. It gives me great peace of mind to know that the government in power is choosing a wise path.
May 21, 1991

The Address

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the Speech from the Throne, and we in the Bloc Quebecois, especially, realized that the emphasis was on the fact that Canadian unity was the only way

May 21, 1991
The Address
to strengthen the Canadian economy or save Canada. They say that without Canadian unity, we won't be able to save this country, we will not make any progress, we will not develop, and they even go so far as to include education.
Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that Canada has been united for at least 20 or 30 years and things are not bad. However, in the process we have managed to go into debt to the tune of $20 to $30 billion annually. That is the only way this country has been united.
So far, as everybody is aware, and especially members of this House, Canada is facing a deficit of $400 billion. To those who may not realize what this means, $400 billion means $400,000 million dollars. Every year, nearly 30 per cent of our income tax and other taxes are used to pay off the interest on the debt alone. A few years from now, this figure will be 50 per cent. As for me, I do not think that the Canadian unity has been well served until now.

The big problem that we are dealing with exists primarily because the union that was seeked, namely the union between Lower and Upper Canada, has become a centralized federalism. At the same time, the provinces and the central government were given powers, thereby setting the stage for regular confrontations. Every day, there is confrontation between the provinces.
At the federal level, members want more and more powers in order to be able to spend more and give theats to the population. This is not necessarily logical; it is not necessarily adequate, but they are only interested in being able to give to the population, in order to win votes. That happens at the federal level.
It is the same with the provinces. In Quebec, for instance they want to regain certain powers in order to be able to give out more money, and to show the population that they have something to offer. That is what brings on confrontation. That is why having 11 jurisdictions in this country is leading us towards catastrophe and bankruptcy. It is essential to decentralize and, we think, go all the way to sovereignty, because in the Meech Lake Accord, Quebec wanted a little more power to function smoothly, just a little bit more power to build a successful society. But no, these minimal requests were rejected. So, Mr. Speaker, what then could do the members of Parliament that were here to defend Quebec's interests in Ottawa? We had no choice
but to resign and form the Bloc Quebecois, as we have done, in order to defend the interests of Quebecers with dignity.
This cannot be done if one belongs to a so-called national party, because when you belong to a so-called national Canadian party, it is impossible to protect the interests of Quebec, since you always have to take into account whether you are likely to win or lose votes in Ontario or in the East.
On the other hand, when we ask questions in the name of Quebec, when we defend the interests of Quebec, those interests are strictly the interests of that province. We are not the least concerned about whether we are going to lose votes in East or in the West.
That is why we can look after the interests of Quebec with dignity. That is also why I ask the Prime Minister of Canada to resign-
